segments.he: אפ"ה פטור וכו' ופי' הסמ"ע מש"ד אבל היסת חייב והב"ח השיג דאף מהיסת פטור והש"ך בס"ק נ"ג הסכים לסמ"ע וכ' שכ"כ הנ"י ואעפ"י שכתב הנ"י שהרשב"א והר"ן דחו ראית הרמב"ן מ"מ יוכל להיות דבדינ' ל"פ עליו וכן אפשר לפ' דעת הטור ולא הבנתי דבריו דבנ"י דהביא מחלוקת הרמב"ן והרשב"א לא ע"ז הביאו רק בדלעיל באומר שתי' אי צריך לישבע היסת או לא בזו נחלקו בראיה אבל זה כבר כ' הטור והמחבר לעיל באומר שתי' דחייב לישבע היסת וא"כ תמהני וביחוד על הב"ח כיון דהעלה הטור במודה רק בשתי' חייב היסת היאך ס"ד במודה בשלשה דפטור מהיסת א"כ אערומ' קמערים אי אמרי' שתי' אצטרך לישבע אמינא שלשה ואהי' פטור מכל וכל ופשיטא דאי בזה חייב היסת אף בזה חייב ושגגה יצא מלפני השליט הב"ח.
segments.en: Even so , he is exempt, etc. The Sema explains that he is exempt from a Torah oath, but he must take a heset oath. The Bach disagrees and holds that he is exempt even from heset. The Shach in seif katan 53 agrees with the Sema and writes that the Nimukei Yosef says the same. Although the Nimukei Yosef writes that the Rashba and the Ran rejected the Ramban’s proof, the Shach suggests that they may nevertheless agree with him as to the law, and that the Tur can likewise be understood this way. I do not understand his words. The dispute brought by the Nimukei Yosef between the Ramban and the Rashba does not concern this case. It concerns the preceding case, where the defendant admits only two, as to whether he must take a heset oath. Yet the Tur and the Mechaber have already ruled above that one who admits two must take heset. I am therefore surprised, especially at the Bach. Since the Tur concludes that one who admits only two must take heset, how could one think that if he admits three he would be exempt even from heset? He could then evade the oath by artifice: if he says two he must swear, so he will say three and be wholly exempt. Plainly, if the former case requires heset, so does this one. The Bach’s ruling was an inadvertent error.

segments.he: או לאביך וכו' הש"ך העתיק בס"ק נ"ה דברי ר"ה גאון ואני אעתיקו בקצרה שורש דבריו יורש שטען היה לאבי בידך ק' זוז והוא אומר אין לו בידי רק חמשי' פטור משבועה דה"ל משיב אבידה אבל אם אמר אמת היה לי מאה מאביך בידי ופרעתיו נו"ן חייב שבועה אם לא שקדמה הודאה לתביעה והוא שלא יהיה כמערים ואם יש עדים או קול שהיה מו"מ בינו לבין המת אף שקדמה הודאה מ"מ חייב עכ"ל בקיצור ודבריו תמוהים דאם פוסק כרבנן דפליגי אראב"י וס"ל בבנו מעיז א"כ אף באומר פרעתיו ה"ל משיב אבידה וכמו כן במ"ש דאם יש עדים וקול דאפילו בהודה קודם לתביעה צריך שבועה למה הא מ"מ משיב אבידה דאף דנימא כדעת הש"ך דעדים מעידים שהלוהו בבירור מ"מ הא הוא משיב אבידה דמצי לומר דפרע הכל דהא בבנו מעיז והש"ך ביקש לפ' דמיירי דיורש טוען ברי שהלוה לך אבי אבל א"י אם פרעת וזה מוסיף תימא יותר דא"כ אין היורש טוען ברי אם פרע או לא פרע וא"כ לכ"ע ליכא כאן שבועה דלא הוי טענת ברי ופשוט וגם ק' הא בגמרא מבואר דטוען פרעתיו כדאמר והאכלתיו פרס ומ"מ ס"ל לרבנן דכוותייהו פסק הגאון דה"ל משיב אבידה. והרב הש"ך חשב דר"ה גאון מפרש דפליגי בקדמה הודאה לתביעה אבל אח"כ חכמים מודים דחייב ש"ד ומלבד דאין זה מועיל דא"כ בקדמה התביעה אפילו באומר לא לויתי רק חמשים דלמא ס"ל לחכמים דחייב אף גם דקשה הך דבעינן התביעה קודם להודאה אין ענין כלל לפלוגתא גבי בנו ה"ל לומר כן בבע"ד עצמו אי בעינן תביעה קודם להודאה או לא. ומה ענין בנו מעיז לכך וזהו כללא הוא כמ"ש הרמב"ן בשם ר"ה גאון דבכ"מ בעינן תביעה קודם להודאה ואין זה ענין מחלוקתם כלל רק פליגי בקדמה תביעה כמ"ש הרמב"ן ולכך אין אני מוצא בכל אריכות הש"ך שמעלה ארוכה אפי' במקצת לדברי הגאון הנ"ל. ומה שנ"ל או דהא דקאמר הגאון ופרעתיו אין פירושו שפרע לאביו רק שפרע ליורש והוא לשון נסתר ולא כמדבר לנוכח והכוונה על היורש ואין זה מהזרות בלשון ר"ה גאון כאשר יעיד כל הוגה בשערי שבועות שלו ואולי ט"ס הוא וצ"ל פרעתיך וס"ל לר"ה גאון כי אמרי' בבנו מעיז היינו באומר אביך לא הלוה לי או לאביך פרעתי והאכלתיו פרס כיון דהם דברים שאין מכחיש ליורש בעצמו ואף דיורש צוח ככרוכי' ידעתי וגם ידעתי דלוה לך או לא היה נפרע ממך יכול להשמט את זה העלם ודבר סתר היה לי אתו ובפניך אמר שמלוה לי ולא היה כן רק לפרעון או למתנה וכדומה וכן בפרעון אטו בכיפי תליא ליה אבל באומר לך פרעתי זהו מהעזה איך יכול החי להכחיש החי ואם כן הרי כאן מודה מקצת וליכא משיב אבידה דהוי ליה העזה: והא ל"א הא יש לו מגו דפרע לאביו דמכל מקום עכשיו הוי מודה מקצת ומגו כזה לפטור משבועה לא אמרינן ויש לר"ה גאון ראיה מהך דפרק הנזקין דאמרינן אם טוענו ב' כיסין מצאת והלה אומר רק א' פטור משבועה דהוי ליה משיב אבידה אבל אם מודה ואמר מצאתי שנים רק כבר נתתי לך אחד חייב לישבע אף דיש לו מגו דהיה אומר לא מצאתי רק אחד מכל מקום עכשיו דמודה דהחזיר אחד והלה כופר הוי ליה מודה במקצת. וע"ש בתו' והיא הדין הכ' דאף דמתחילה היה יכול לומר להד"ם או פרעתי לאביך מ"מ עכשיו שאומר לו פרע והוא מכחישו ה"ל ש"ד. והוא שקדמה תביעה להודאה דאל"כ בכל מ"מ פטור ומכ"ש בזה רק הוסיף דאם יש עדים או קול נראה דכוונתו להערים פן יתבענו היורש ולכך הקדים הודאה לתביעה וה"ל כקדמה תביעה וחייב וא"ש דברי ר"ה גאון ואין בו מהזרות וזה נראה לפי שיטת הש"ך. אך יותר נראה פשוט כי ודאי ש"ד לעול' פטור דכיון דקי"ל כרבנן דבבנו מעיז רק מהיסת לא ימלט אם בנו תבעו רק ר"ה ס"ל כמ"ש התו' בב"ק והמרדכי בפ' כל הנשבעין דפסק ר"ה גאון כלישנא בתרא דר"נ דאין היסת רק בדררא דממון וא"כ א"ש ביורש התובע וטוען ברי מנה לאבא בידך והוא אומר א"ח רק חמשים ליכא כאן מ"מ דבבנו מעיז וגם היסת ליכא דהא אמר מעולם לא לוה רק חמשים אבל אם אמר אמת לויתי ק' רק פרעתיו חמשים א"כ אף דאין כאן ש"ד מ"מ היסת חייב דבפרעון ה"ל דררא דממון ומחייב ר"נ היסת והנ"מ בקדמה תביעה אבל בקדמה הודאה ה"ל משיב אבידה ואפי' מהיסת פטור דאם היה שותק לא היה תובעו כלל ולכך התנה שלא יהיו עדים וקול דאל"כ לא הוי משיב אבידה דידע דבנו יתבע הוגד לי וכדומה ומערים להקדים להודות והרי חייב היסת ודברי ר"ה ברורים ופשוטים ונכונים: וא"כ לדינא אף דקי"ל כר"נ אפילו בדליכא דררא דממון מ"מ זה למדנו דמ"ש בש"ע דהוי משיב אבידה בדליכא קול אבל בדאיכא קול לא מהימן בלי היסת דאין זה משיב אבידה וצ"ע. הואיל ולא העתיקו המחברים אבל לענ"ד כוונתי לקוטב האמת בכוונת ר"ה גאון ז"ל:
segments.en: Or to your father, etc. The Shach in seif katan 55 quotes the words of Rav Hai Gaon. I will state their essential point briefly. If an heir claims, “You had one hundred zuz belonging to my father,” and the defendant says, “I have only fifty of his,” he is exempt from an oath because he is returning a lost object. But if he says, “It is true that I had one hundred of your father’s in my possession, but I repaid fifty,” he must swear, unless his admission preceded the claim, provided that he is not acting deceptively. If there are witnesses or a public report that he had financial dealings with the deceased, then even if his admission preceded the claim he must swear. These words are puzzling. If Rav Hai Gaon rules like the Sages who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and hold that a person can brazenly deny a claim made by the creditor’s son, then even when he says, “I repaid fifty,” he should be regarded as returning a lost object. Likewise, why does Rav Hai say that where there are witnesses or a public report he must swear even if his admission preceded the claim? He is still returning a lost object. Even if, as the Shach understands, witnesses establish with certainty that the deceased lent him the money, he could still have claimed that he repaid the entire amount, since according to the Sages a person is capable of brazenly denying the son. The Shach attempts to explain that the heir claims with certainty that his father lent the money, but does not know whether it was repaid. This makes the matter even more difficult. The heir then has no definite claim regarding repayment, and according to everyone no oath can be imposed because there is no definite claim. Moreover, the Gemara itself speaks of a defendant who claims repayment, saying, “I fed him half,” and nevertheless the Sages, whose view Rav Hai follows, consider him one who returns a lost object. The Shach thought that Rav Hai understands the dispute as concerning whether the admission preceded the claim, while the Sages would agree that if the claim came first a Torah oath is required. Apart from the fact that this does not solve the problem, for then even if the defendant said merely, “I never borrowed more than fifty,” perhaps the Sages would obligate him once the claim preceded the admission, the distinction between a claim preceding the admission and an admission preceding the claim has no special connection to the dispute concerning a creditor’s son. The same issue would apply between the original litigants themselves. The Ramban, in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, indeed states as a general rule that an admission of part generates an oath only when the claim precedes the admission. That principle is independent of the dispute here, which itself concerns a case where the claim did precede the admission. Thus, despite the Shach’s lengthy discussion, I do not find that he has resolved even part of the Gaon’s words. One possible explanation is that Rav Hai’s phrase “and he repaid him” does not mean that the defendant repaid the father. It means that he repaid the heir. The language is in the third person rather than addressing the heir directly, but such usage is not unusual in Rav Hai Gaon’s Sha’arei Shevuot, as anyone familiar with that work will recognize. Perhaps there is simply a scribal error and the text should read, “I repaid you.” Rav Hai would then hold that when we say a person can brazenly deny the son, that applies where he says, “Your father never lent me,” or, “I repaid your father,” because these assertions do not directly contradict the heir himself. Even if the heir cries out that he knows the loan occurred and knows that his father was not repaid, the defendant can evade the accusation by saying that there were private matters between himself and the father. The father’s statement in the son’s presence that the money was a loan may have been inaccurate, or the transfer may have been repayment, a gift, or something similar. Likewise, repayment to the father need not have occurred openly. But if the defendant says to the heir, “I repaid you,” that is a direct act of brazenness. How can one living person deny another living person to his face regarding a payment supposedly made directly to him? In that case the defendant is one who admits part of the claim, and he is not regarded as returning a lost object, because his present defense is brazen. We do not say that he has a migo that he could have claimed that he repaid the father. Once he presently admits part of the claim, such a migo does not exempt him from the oath imposed upon one who admits part. Rav Hai has support from the chapter HaNizakin. There, if the claimant says, “You found two purses,” and the finder says, “I found only one,” he is exempt because he is returning a lost object. But if he admits, “I found two, but I already gave one back to you,” he must swear, even though he has a migo that he could have said, “I found only one.” Since he now admits finding two and claims to have returned one, while the claimant denies receiving it, he is one who admits part of the claim. See Tosafot there. The same applies here. Even though he initially could have said that no loan occurred or that he repaid the father, once he says that he repaid the heir and the heir directly denies it, a Torah oath applies. This is provided that the claim preceded the admission. Otherwise, an admission of part made before any claim generally does not create an oath, and certainly not here. Rav Hai adds that if there are witnesses or a public report, it appears that the defendant is acting deceptively, anticipating that the heir will claim against him and therefore hastening to make an admission before the formal claim. Such a preemptive admission is treated like one made after a claim, and he must swear. On the Shach’s approach, Rav Hai’s words can therefore be understood without any unusual result. A simpler explanation, however, appears more likely. Rav Hai certainly does not impose a Torah oath in this case at all. Since we rule like the Sages that a person can brazenly deny the son, the defendant is exempt from a Torah oath. The entire question concerns heset. Rav Hai holds, as Tosafot in Bava Kamma and the Mordechai in the chapter Kol HaNishba’in report in his name, that the halakhah follows the second version of Rav Nachman, under which heset was instituted only where there is a concrete basis for a monetary claim. Accordingly, where the heir claims with certainty, “You owe my father one hundred,” and the defendant says, “I owe only fifty, because I never borrowed more than fifty,” there is no admission of part for a Torah oath, since one may brazenly deny the son. There is also no heset under Rav Hai’s rule, because with respect to the denied fifty there is no concrete basis for the claim. But if the defendant says, “It is true that I borrowed one hundred, but I repaid fifty,” then although there is still no Torah oath, heset is required. A repayment defense creates a concrete monetary basis, and Rav Nachman imposed heset in such a case. This distinction applies where the claim preceded the admission. If the defendant first volunteered the admission before the heir claimed anything, he is returning a lost object and is exempt even from heset, because had he remained silent the heir might never have demanded anything. Rav Hai therefore adds that there must be no witnesses or public report. If witnesses or a public report exist, the defendant cannot be considered a genuine returner of a lost object, since he knows that the heir is likely to hear of the transaction and make a claim. His early admission may be an artifice designed to precede the claim. He therefore remains obligated in heset. On this reading Rav Hai Gaon’s words are clear, straightforward, and correct. As a matter of practical law, although we rule like Rav Nachman that heset applies even where there is no prior concrete basis for the monetary claim, we nevertheless learn from Rav Hai an important qualification to the Mechaber’s ruling. The Mechaber treats the defendant as one who returns a lost object where there is no public report. Where such a report exists, however, he should not be believed without heset, because he is not truly returning a lost object. This requires study because the later authorities did not reproduce the qualification, but in my view this is the central and correct intent of Rav Hai Gaon.

segments.he: פטור ואפי' משבועת היסת הש"ך תמה למה יפטור מהיסת כי הרמב"ן נתן טעם דמשום דקדמה הודאה לתביעה וזהו טעם שאין בו ש"ד אבל היסת למה לא. ודבריו בלתי ברורים דהא באומר שני כיסין מצאתי והחזרתי לך אחד מהם והלה כופר לא החזרת לי אף דטענו עכשיו ברי מתוך הודאתו דחייב לו עוד כיס אחד מ"מ הואיל אלו שתק לא היה נוטל כלום ה"ל משיב אבידה ופטור אפי' מהיסת וכ"פ הרמב"ם והטור והמחבר לקמן סי' רס"ז ע"ש וא"כ היינו הך דעכשיו טוען ברי שלא פרעתני מ"מ אלו שתק אפי' מקצת לא הגיע לו דהא לא היה יודע כלל שחבירו חייב לו א"כ ה"ל משיב אבידה ואפילו מהיסת פטור ועיין בבעה"ת שער ז' ח"ב דמדמי הך לשני כיסין וכו' באמת שוים הם בדין ובסברא ולכן אין כאן פקפוק כלל. וכתב הש"ך בס"ק נ"ד בשם רי"ו דכתב דאם מתוך הודאתו נתברר לו דחייב ברי ומקדם לא היה תביעתו רק בשמא דעת רש"י בגיטין פ' הנזיקין דהוי ש"ד וחלקו עליו גדולי מורי'. ואני תמה דאין לכאורה מדברי רש"י ראי' לדינא דאמת דרש"י כתב כן במילתא דר' יצחק האומר שני כיסין מצאת והלה אומר לא מצאתי אלא אחד ישבע דכיסין לא מנתקי מהדדי ופירש"י דלא ראה וידע שמצאם רק הוא אמר שמצא כיס א' וטוען הוא עליו לדברך שנים מצאת ישבע הרי דס"ל דכה"ג הוי מודה מקצת. אבל קשה הא הוי משיב אבידה והוא בכלל מוצא אבידה לא ישבע כמ"ש רש"י בכמה דוכתי ואי שתק לא ה"ל כלום ורש"י לא אמרה אלא במילתא דר' יצחק דאיהו לא ס"ל הך משנה דלא ישבע מפני ת"ע כמבואר בגמרא ויפה פירש רש"י אבל לפי דקיי"ל כמשנה דמוצא מציאה לא ישבע אף בזו לא ישבע לדינא וא"כ רי"ו העתיק דברי רש"י לדינא ואינו וצ"ע לכאורה:
segments.en: He is exempt , even from a heset oath. The Shach asks why he should be exempt from heset. The Ramban’s reason is that the admission preceded the claim, which explains why there is no Torah oath, but why should heset also be absent? His objection is not clear. If one says, “I found two purses and returned one to you,” and the claimant denies that any purse was returned, then although the claimant now has a definite claim based upon the finder’s own admission, since had the finder remained silent the claimant would have received nothing, the finder is regarded as returning a lost object and is exempt even from heset. The Rambam, Tur, and Mechaber all rule this way below in siman 267. The present case is identical. The claimant now says with certainty, “You did not repay me,” but had the defendant remained silent the claimant would not have received even part of the money, because he did not know at all that the other person owed him anything. The defendant is therefore returning a lost object and is exempt even from heset. See Baal HaTerumot, Sha’ar 7, part 2, which indeed compares this case to the two purses. They are identical both in law and in reasoning, and there is no difficulty. The Shach in seif katan 54 cites Rabbenu Yerucham, who writes that if the claimant’s certainty arose only from the defendant’s admission, whereas his earlier claim had been merely uncertain, Rashi’s view in the chapter HaNizakin is that a Torah oath applies, though Rabbenu Yerucham’s great teachers disagreed. At first glance I am surprised, because Rashi’s words do not appear to prove such a practical ruling. Rashi explains Rabbi Yitzchak’s case where the claimant says, “You found two purses,” and the defendant says, “I found only one,” and must swear because purses are not usually separated from one another. Rashi explains that the claimant did not actually see or know that the finder found them. Rather, the finder admitted finding one purse, and the claimant then said, “According to your own words, you found two.” Rashi thus holds that this can constitute an admission of part. But there is an obvious difficulty. The finder is returning a lost object, and the Mishnah states that one who returns a lost object does not swear, as Rashi himself explains in several places. Had the finder remained silent the claimant would have had nothing. Rashi said what he did only in explaining Rabbi Yitzchak’s own statement. Rabbi Yitzchak does not accept the Mishnah’s exemption for a finder based upon the concern for tikkun olam, as is evident in the Gemara. Rashi therefore explained Rabbi Yitzchak correctly. According to the halakhah, however, we follow the Mishnah that a finder does not swear. Even in this case he should therefore not swear as a practical matter. If Rabbenu Yerucham copied Rashi’s explanation as a practical ruling, that appears difficult and requires study. What appears possible in defense of Rabbenu Yerucham is as follows. Rashi does not read the Gemara’s continuation with the text “this was also taught,” as Tosafot do. This raises the question: according to whom does Rabbi Yitzchak state his rule?

segments.he: ומה שנראה דס"ל לרי"ו דלרש"י דלא גרס תנ"ה כגי' התו' א"כ קשה ר"י דאמר כמאן ועכצ"ל דס"ל דבמסקנא תליא דלראב"י דס"ל בבנו אין מעיז אף דלא קיבל מידו דבר מ"מ אינו מעיז א"כ אף באבידה לא יעיז להחזיק לעצמו האבידה דס"ל העזה כר"ת אף דאין חבירו מכיר בשקרו כמש"ל בכללי מגו באריכות ע"ש סי' קי"ב וקי"ג ולשמא לא יגביהנה לא חיישינן דמהכ"ת לא יגביהנה אולי של נכרי היא או של ישראל ונתוודע דכבר נתייאשו הבעלים טרם שמצאה והרי הוא שלו. וא"כ לא שייך ת"ע כלל ולכך ס"ל לר"י ישבע אבל לרבנן דס"ל בבנו מעיז הואיל ולא קיבל ממנו מעות ומכ"ש באבידה וא"כ יש חשש ת"ע ולכך לא ישבע. ולפ"ז אם הוא לא ידע שהלוהו והוא מודה לו שהלוהו רק פרעתי מחצה והלה אומר ברי לי שלא פרעתני כלל לכ"ע לא הוי ת"ע דהא לשמא לא יגביהנה לא חיישינן רק שמא לא יחזירנו וכאן הא הוי העזה אף דאינו מכיר בשקרו ואי דלא קיבל הימנו ה"מ בבנו אבל בעצמו הא קיבל ממנו וכ"ע מודים לדר' יצחק דלא הוי ת"ע ולכך ישבע זהו מה שנ"ל להליץ בעד רבינו ירוחם וצ"ע. ודברי מהרש"א בפ"ב דכתובות נוטי' לכך דתי' על קושית מהרש"ל דלתני לראב"י מודה ר' יהושע בדלא תבעו ותי' מהרש"א דאם יש עדים לא מתוקמא ע"ש ולכאורה דבריו בלתי מובנים דהא כך ענין הקו' דליתני מוד' ר"י בדלא תבע ולא ידע שחייב והוא מעצמו הודה שחייב מנה רק פרע נו"ן ועכצ"ל דאח"כ תובע ואמר ברי שלא פרעתני דאל"כ הא אין כאן טענת ברי לחייב שבועה ומה ארי' משום פה שאסר וכו' וא"כ דטוען ברי אין כאן מגו רק דשתק ולא הודה כלל דחייב וא"כ א"ש דאם יש עדים דלוה הימנו א"כ אין כאן מגו כלל דבפרעון הא טוען ברי לא פרעת ועל גוף הלואה הא יש עדים וצ"ע לכאורה ולפי הנ"ל ניחא דבלא"ה אם נתפוש לאמת כדעת רי"ו הא לראב"י שוה הבן להוא בעצמו דמ"ש דהא ס"ל אף בבנו א"מ וא"כ משפט א' לכולם אם לא תבעו ואח"כ מתוך הודאתו נתברר לו דחייב הוי מ"מ וחייב שבועה וא"כ מה קו' דלתני מודה ר' בדלא תבעו רק מעצמו אמר מנה לאבא בידך וכו' דע"כ איירי דאח"כ טוען ברי לא פרעת כלל דאל"כ בלא"ה לא חייב שבועה דאין כאן טענת ברי וא"כ הא באמת חייב שבועה כמ"ש רי"ו לדעת רש"י ואיך נתנו מודה ר"י דפטור הא לא כן הוא ואין כאן מקום כלל לקו' מהרש"ל ומהרש"א אמנם נראה דס"ל כדעת האומרי' דל"פ ראב"י וחכמים אלא בטוען עומד הייתי וראיתי דלא פרע כי לא זז ידי מתוך ידו וכדומה אבל באומר כך אמר לי אבא אף ראב"י מודה דמעיז ויש להם ראיה מהא דמשני בשבועה רישא דקתני מנה לאביך בידך והאכלתיו פרס דפטור דהוי משיב אבידה דאיירי בדלא טען ברי וק' אם לא טוען ברי כלל רק שמא מאי ארי' דהוי משיב אבידה הא אין נשבעים על טענת שמא וכן הק' במרדכי פ' הנ"ל ועכצ"ל דלא טען ברי עומד הייתי רק טוען ברי אמר לי ומודה ראב"י דהוי משיב אבידה וצ"ל דאמר לי אבא הוי טענת ברי לזקוק שבועה דאל"כ עדיין ק' מה ארי' דהוי משיב אבידה ת"ל דאין בטענתו ממש להשביע ולפ"ז ס"ל למהרש"א אי הקו' דלתני מודה ר"י בדלא תבעו ואמר מנה לאביך בידי ופרעתי מחצה והלה טוען עומד הייתי דלא פרע אין כאן קו' דהא בזה באמת לראב"י חייב שבועה כדעת רי"ו וא"כ איך לתני מודה ר"י דפטור ואי הקו' דטען אמר לי אבא דאף ראב"י מודה דמעיז וא"כ ליכא כאן שבועה מפני משיב אבידה דהא מעיז אבל לולי כן חייב דטענתו ברי א"כ שפיר תי' המהרש"א דא"כ איך קתני אם יש עדים דמה בכך דעדים מעידי' על הלואה הא יוכל לומר פרעתיך כולו דבבנו מעיז אף לראב"י אם אין טוען עומד הייתי ודברי המהרש"א ברורים ומוכרחים דס"ל בדעת רש"י כרי"ו. ונראה דהרא"ש בגיטין דכתב דהרי"ף דס"ל דר"י לא אתי' כראב"י לפי מסקנא דקיי"ל בבנו מעיז פליגי ס"ל דלא כפי' רש"י דס"ל אף במסקנא איירי בטענו קטן הואיל דהנתינה בגדלות והדבר תמוה דמנ"מ בזה וכמ"ש המהרש"א להדי' דאף לרש"י אין ענין הך דר"י לראב"י ונראה דוודאי הרא"ש ס"ל בטוענו גדול ע"כ איירי בטוען ברי לי מפי אבא ולא עומד הייתי דאל"כ אמאי קרי לי' קטן דבמילתא דאבוה קטן הוא הא בעומד הרי הוא לא בא במילתא דאבוה דהא בעצמו רא' וע"כ דטען רק כך אמר לי אבא ולכך מתואר בתואר קטן הואיל דנשען על מילתא דאבוה ובהכי ניחא להך שיטה דעומד ורא' חכמים מודים למה מוקמינן הך משנה דשבועות נשבעים לקטן ראב"י היא ולא חכמים בעומד ורואה דא"כ ל"ש במילתא דאבו' קטן הוא וא"כ איך קתני במשנה נשבעים לקטן אך זהו אם הוא באמת גדול אבל לפרש"י דהוא קטן באמת שפיר י"ל עומד ורוא' ונקרא קטן היותו קטן והנה ודאי ס"ל להרא"ש דיש לדמות כהנ"ל אם בבנו מעיז אף במציעה מעיז ויש לחוש שמא לא יחזירנה אבל אם א"מ אף במציא' ל"ל שלא יחזירנה כנ"ל אך אם אמרי' בעומד ורואה לכ"ע אפי' בבנו א"מ ובמציאה איירי בעומד ורואה כמ"ש מהרש"ל והרשב"א דעמד בגגו ורא' מגביה וא"כ א"ש דלרש"י שפיר י"ל דדמי להדדי דאף בבנו ועומד ורוא' מעיז ול"ק למה קתני קטן דהוא באמת קטן משא"כ לדעת התו' קשה למה קרוי קטן ועכצ"ל כהנ"ל דלא מיירי בעומד ורואה רק נסמך על דברי אביו כנ"ל ולא דמי' אבידה כלל להך דבנו מעיז בשום אופן ודוק:
segments.en: One must say that Rashi understands the final conclusion to depend upon the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Sages. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that a person does not brazenly deny the creditor’s son even though he did not receive the money directly from the son. If so, in a lost object case as well he would not brazenly retain the lost object for himself. His concept of brazenness follows Rabbenu Tam, who holds that it is considered brazenness even when the claimant cannot personally recognize the lie, as I explained at length in the rules of migo, simanim 112 and 113. We do not worry that perhaps the finder would simply refrain from picking up the object. Why should he not pick it up? It may belong to a non Jew, or it may belong to a Jew where the finder discovers that the owner had already despaired before he found it, in which case it belongs to the finder. Accordingly, for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov there is no concern for tikkun olam that imposing an oath will deter finders from returning lost property. Rabbi Yitzchak can therefore require an oath. The Sages, however, hold that a person can brazenly deny the creditor’s son because he did not receive the money directly from him. Certainly they would say the same of a lost object. There is therefore a real concern for tikkun olam, and the finder does not swear. According to this, if the claimant originally did not know that the defendant had borrowed from him, and the defendant himself admits the loan but says, “I repaid half,” after which the claimant says with certainty, “I know you did not repay me at all,” there is no tikkun olam concern according to anyone. The concern is not that a person will refrain from taking possession of the object in the first place, only that he might refrain from returning it. Here, withholding repayment is a direct act of brazenness. Although the claimant may not independently know the defendant’s falsehood, the defendant received the money directly from him. The principle that one may brazenly deny because he did not receive anything from the claimant applies only to a son, whereas here the original creditor himself gave the money. Everyone therefore agrees with Rabbi Yitzchak that the tikkun olam rationale does not exempt the defendant, and he must swear. This, in my view, is the best defense of Rabbenu Yerucham, though it still requires study. The Maharsha’s words in the second chapter of Ketubot also tend in this direction. He addresses the Maharshal’s question that the Mishnah could have taught, according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, that Rabbi Yehoshua concedes where the claimant had not first made a demand. The Maharsha answers that the case cannot be established where witnesses exist. At first glance this answer is difficult to understand. The proposed case is that the claimant made no demand and did not know that anything was owed to him. The defendant voluntarily admitted owing one hundred but claimed that he had repaid fifty. Necessarily, the claimant then says with certainty that the fifty was not repaid, because otherwise there would be no definite claim capable of generating an oath. If he now has a definite claim, the defendant’s only migo is that he could have remained silent and never admitted the debt. If witnesses establish the original loan, that migo indeed disappears, because the defendant cannot deny the loan, while the claimant directly denies repayment. This seems to explain the Maharsha’s answer. According to the approach above, however, the matter is clearer. If Rabbenu Yerucham is correct, then according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov the son is treated like the original creditor, because Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that even toward the son the defendant does not brazenly deny. Thus, if no claim was initially made and the claimant’s certainty arose only from the defendant’s admission, the defendant is still one who admits part and must swear. What then is the Maharshal’s question that the Mishnah should teach that Rabbi Yehoshua concedes and exempts him where the claim was not made first? Necessarily, after the voluntary admission the claimant would have to say with certainty that no repayment occurred. But in precisely that case, according to Rabbenu Yerucham’s reading of Rashi, a Torah oath applies. There is therefore no possible formulation in which Rabbi Yehoshua would concede exemption, and the Maharshal’s question would never arise. It appears, however, that the Maharsha follows those authorities who hold that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Sages disagree only where the son says, “I stood there and saw that you did not repay, because I never moved away from them,” or an equivalent claim based upon his own observation. If the son says only, “My father told me so,” then even Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agrees that the defendant can be brazen toward him. They derive this from the Gemara in Shevuot, where the first clause, “I owe your father one hundred and fed him half,” is exempt because the defendant is returning a lost object, and the Gemara establishes it as a case where the son did not make a fully independent definite claim. If the son’s claim were wholly uncertain, however, why would the Gemara need the reason that the defendant is returning a lost object? No oath is imposed on an uncertain claim in any event, as the Mordechai asks. One must therefore say that the son’s claim is definite in the sense that he says, “My father told me,” yet it is not based upon his own observation. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agrees that in such a case the defendant can be brazen toward the son. At the same time, the statement “my father told me” is sufficiently definite to support an oath where the other requirements exist, for otherwise the Gemara could simply have said that the claim itself is insufficient rather than invoking the lost object rationale. Accordingly, the Maharsha can distinguish two versions of the Maharshal’s proposed case. If the defendant voluntarily says, “I owe your father one hundred but repaid fifty,” and the son says, “I stood there and saw that you never repaid,” there is no question at all. According to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov the defendant must indeed swear, exactly as Rabbenu Yerucham maintains, so the Mishnah could not present this as a case in which Rabbi Yehoshua concedes exemption. If instead the son says only, “My father told me that you did not repay,” then even Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agrees that the defendant can brazenly deny him. In that setting there would be no oath because the defendant is returning a lost object, although absent that rationale the son’s statement is a definite claim. The Maharsha therefore correctly answers that such a case cannot be reconciled with the clause involving witnesses. If witnesses establish the loan, the defendant can still say that he repaid the entire amount to the father, because even according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov he can brazenly deny the son where the son did not personally observe the matter. Thus the witnesses would not produce the result stated in the Mishnah. The Maharsha’s words are therefore clear and compelling, and they assume Rabbenu Yerucham’s understanding of Rashi. The Rosh in Gittin writes that the Rif, who holds that Rabbi Yitzchak’s rule does not accord with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov after the Gemara concludes that a person can be brazen toward the son, does not follow Rashi’s explanation. Rashi maintains that even at the conclusion the case concerns an actual minor, because the lost object was handed over after the claimant had reached adulthood. This is difficult. What practical difference should the claimant’s actual age make? The Maharsha explicitly writes that even according to Rashi, Rabbi Yitzchak’s rule is not inherently tied to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. It seems that the Rosh understood that if the claimant is an adult, the case necessarily concerns one who claims with certainty based upon what his father told him, rather than one who personally stood and saw the event. Otherwise, why would the Gemara call him “a minor in his father’s matter”? If he personally saw everything, his claim is not dependent upon his father’s matter at all. He is called a minor in his father’s matter precisely because his knowledge rests upon his father’s statement. This also resolves another point. According to the view that the Sages agree that a defendant cannot brazenly deny the son where the son personally stood and saw, why does the Gemara establish the Mishnah in Shevuot concerning oaths to a minor specifically according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rather than the Sages, by saying that the son stood and saw? If the claimant is truly an adult, that would not fit the Mishnah’s designation “a minor in his father’s matter,” because his claim rests on his own observation. According to Rashi, however, the claimant is an actual minor. It is therefore entirely possible that he stood and saw and is still called a minor simply because of his age. The Rosh certainly understood the comparison stated above. If a defendant can brazenly deny the son, he can likewise brazenly retain a found object, creating the concern that an oath will deter him from returning it. If he cannot brazenly deny the son, there is no comparable concern regarding a found object. But where the son personally stood and saw, everyone agrees that the defendant cannot brazenly deny him, and the lost object case likewise concerns one who stood and saw, as the Maharshal and Rashba explain, such as where the claimant stood on his roof and saw the finder lift the object. Rashi can therefore compare the two cases because even with a son who personally observed the matter the defendant can be brazen if the son is an actual minor. According to Tosafot, however, the claimant is not an actual minor, and the phrase “minor in his father’s matter” must mean that his knowledge depends upon his father’s report. The lost object case, which involves direct observation, is therefore not comparable to the case of the son at all. Examine this carefully.

segments.he: (כאן חסר בדברי רבינו עלה א' וחבל על דאבדין וכדהוינא טלי' וזכיתי לשאוב מים חיים מבאר הקבוע לרבי' של אמו"ז הגאון זצלה"ה שמעתי ממנו מקצת דמקצת והמה חקוק אצלי לזכרון בעלמא אמרתי להעתיקה פה מבלי לאבד מדברי קדשו)
segments.en: Here one page is missing from our master’s words. It is a loss to be regretted. When I was young I merited to draw living waters from the well of my maternal grandfather, our master the gaon, of blessed memory. I heard from him a small portion of these matters, and because they remain engraved in my memory I have copied them here so that his holy words should not be lost.

en_segments: Even so , he is exempt, etc. The Sema explains that he is exempt from a Torah oath, but he must take a heset oath. The Bach disagrees and holds that he is exempt even from heset. The Shach in seif katan 53 agrees with the Sema and writes that the Nimukei Yosef says the same. Although the Nimukei Yosef writes that the Rashba and the Ran rejected the Ramban’s proof, the Shach suggests that they may nevertheless agree with him as to the law, and that the Tur can likewise be understood this way. I do not understand his words. The dispute brought by the Nimukei Yosef between the Ramban and the Rashba does not concern this case. It concerns the preceding case, where the defendant admits only two, as to whether he must take a heset oath. Yet the Tur and the Mechaber have already ruled above that one who admits two must take heset. I am therefore surprised, especially at the Bach. Since the Tur concludes that one who admits only two must take heset, how could one think that if he admits three he would be exempt even from heset? He could then evade the oath by artifice: if he says two he must swear, so he will say three and be wholly exempt. Plainly, if the former case requires heset, so does this one. The Bach’s ruling was an inadvertent error.

Or to your father, etc. The Shach in seif katan 55 quotes the words of Rav Hai Gaon. I will state their essential point briefly. If an heir claims, “You had one hundred zuz belonging to my father,” and the defendant says, “I have only fifty of his,” he is exempt from an oath because he is returning a lost object. But if he says, “It is true that I had one hundred of your father’s in my possession, but I repaid fifty,” he must swear, unless his admission preceded the claim, provided that he is not acting deceptively. If there are witnesses or a public report that he had financial dealings with the deceased, then even if his admission preceded the claim he must swear. These words are puzzling. If Rav Hai Gaon rules like the Sages who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and hold that a person can brazenly deny a claim made by the creditor’s son, then even when he says, “I repaid fifty,” he should be regarded as returning a lost object. Likewise, why does Rav Hai say that where there are witnesses or a public report he must swear even if his admission preceded the claim? He is still returning a lost object. Even if, as the Shach understands, witnesses establish with certainty that the deceased lent him the money, he could still have claimed that he repaid the entire amount, since according to the Sages a person is capable of brazenly denying the son. The Shach attempts to explain that the heir claims with certainty that his father lent the money, but does not know whether it was repaid. This makes the matter even more difficult. The heir then has no definite claim regarding repayment, and according to everyone no oath can be imposed because there is no definite claim. Moreover, the Gemara itself speaks of a defendant who claims repayment, saying, “I fed him half,” and nevertheless the Sages, whose view Rav Hai follows, consider him one who returns a lost object. The Shach thought that Rav Hai understands the dispute as concerning whether the admission preceded the claim, while the Sages would agree that if the claim came first a Torah oath is required. Apart from the fact that this does not solve the problem, for then even if the defendant said merely, “I never borrowed more than fifty,” perhaps the Sages would obligate him once the claim preceded the admission, the distinction between a claim preceding the admission and an admission preceding the claim has no special connection to the dispute concerning a creditor’s son. The same issue would apply between the original litigants themselves. The Ramban, in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, indeed states as a general rule that an admission of part generates an oath only when the claim precedes the admission. That principle is independent of the dispute here, which itself concerns a case where the claim did precede the admission. Thus, despite the Shach’s lengthy discussion, I do not find that he has resolved even part of the Gaon’s words. One possible explanation is that Rav Hai’s phrase “and he repaid him” does not mean that the defendant repaid the father. It means that he repaid the heir. The language is in the third person rather than addressing the heir directly, but such usage is not unusual in Rav Hai Gaon’s Sha’arei Shevuot, as anyone familiar with that work will recognize. Perhaps there is simply a scribal error and the text should read, “I repaid you.” Rav Hai would then hold that when we say a person can brazenly deny the son, that applies where he says, “Your father never lent me,” or, “I repaid your father,” because these assertions do not directly contradict the heir himself. Even if the heir cries out that he knows the loan occurred and knows that his father was not repaid, the defendant can evade the accusation by saying that there were private matters between himself and the father. The father’s statement in the son’s presence that the money was a loan may have been inaccurate, or the transfer may have been repayment, a gift, or something similar. Likewise, repayment to the father need not have occurred openly. But if the defendant says to the heir, “I repaid you,” that is a direct act of brazenness. How can one living person deny another living person to his face regarding a payment supposedly made directly to him? In that case the defendant is one who admits part of the claim, and he is not regarded as returning a lost object, because his present defense is brazen. We do not say that he has a migo that he could have claimed that he repaid the father. Once he presently admits part of the claim, such a migo does not exempt him from the oath imposed upon one who admits part. Rav Hai has support from the chapter HaNizakin. There, if the claimant says, “You found two purses,” and the finder says, “I found only one,” he is exempt because he is returning a lost object. But if he admits, “I found two, but I already gave one back to you,” he must swear, even though he has a migo that he could have said, “I found only one.” Since he now admits finding two and claims to have returned one, while the claimant denies receiving it, he is one who admits part of the claim. See Tosafot there. The same applies here. Even though he initially could have said that no loan occurred or that he repaid the father, once he says that he repaid the heir and the heir directly denies it, a Torah oath applies. This is provided that the claim preceded the admission. Otherwise, an admission of part made before any claim generally does not create an oath, and certainly not here. Rav Hai adds that if there are witnesses or a public report, it appears that the defendant is acting deceptively, anticipating that the heir will claim against him and therefore hastening to make an admission before the formal claim. Such a preemptive admission is treated like one made after a claim, and he must swear. On the Shach’s approach, Rav Hai’s words can therefore be understood without any unusual result. A simpler explanation, however, appears more likely. Rav Hai certainly does not impose a Torah oath in this case at all. Since we rule like the Sages that a person can brazenly deny the son, the defendant is exempt from a Torah oath. The entire question concerns heset. Rav Hai holds, as Tosafot in Bava Kamma and the Mordechai in the chapter Kol HaNishba’in report in his name, that the halakhah follows the second version of Rav Nachman, under which heset was instituted only where there is a concrete basis for a monetary claim. Accordingly, where the heir claims with certainty, “You owe my father one hundred,” and the defendant says, “I owe only fifty, because I never borrowed more than fifty,” there is no admission of part for a Torah oath, since one may brazenly deny the son. There is also no heset under Rav Hai’s rule, because with respect to the denied fifty there is no concrete basis for the claim. But if the defendant says, “It is true that I borrowed one hundred, but I repaid fifty,” then although there is still no Torah oath, heset is required. A repayment defense creates a concrete monetary basis, and Rav Nachman imposed heset in such a case. This distinction applies where the claim preceded the admission. If the defendant first volunteered the admission before the heir claimed anything, he is returning a lost object and is exempt even from heset, because had he remained silent the heir might never have demanded anything. Rav Hai therefore adds that there must be no witnesses or public report. If witnesses or a public report exist, the defendant cannot be considered a genuine returner of a lost object, since he knows that the heir is likely to hear of the transaction and make a claim. His early admission may be an artifice designed to precede the claim. He therefore remains obligated in heset. On this reading Rav Hai Gaon’s words are clear, straightforward, and correct. As a matter of practical law, although we rule like Rav Nachman that heset applies even where there is no prior concrete basis for the monetary claim, we nevertheless learn from Rav Hai an important qualification to the Mechaber’s ruling. The Mechaber treats the defendant as one who returns a lost object where there is no public report. Where such a report exists, however, he should not be believed without heset, because he is not truly returning a lost object. This requires study because the later authorities did not reproduce the qualification, but in my view this is the central and correct intent of Rav Hai Gaon.

He is exempt , even from a heset oath. The Shach asks why he should be exempt from heset. The Ramban’s reason is that the admission preceded the claim, which explains why there is no Torah oath, but why should heset also be absent? His objection is not clear. If one says, “I found two purses and returned one to you,” and the claimant denies that any purse was returned, then although the claimant now has a definite claim based upon the finder’s own admission, since had the finder remained silent the claimant would have received nothing, the finder is regarded as returning a lost object and is exempt even from heset. The Rambam, Tur, and Mechaber all rule this way below in siman 267. The present case is identical. The claimant now says with certainty, “You did not repay me,” but had the defendant remained silent the claimant would not have received even part of the money, because he did not know at all that the other person owed him anything. The defendant is therefore returning a lost object and is exempt even from heset. See Baal HaTerumot, Sha’ar 7, part 2, which indeed compares this case to the two purses. They are identical both in law and in reasoning, and there is no difficulty. The Shach in seif katan 54 cites Rabbenu Yerucham, who writes that if the claimant’s certainty arose only from the defendant’s admission, whereas his earlier claim had been merely uncertain, Rashi’s view in the chapter HaNizakin is that a Torah oath applies, though Rabbenu Yerucham’s great teachers disagreed. At first glance I am surprised, because Rashi’s words do not appear to prove such a practical ruling. Rashi explains Rabbi Yitzchak’s case where the claimant says, “You found two purses,” and the defendant says, “I found only one,” and must swear because purses are not usually separated from one another. Rashi explains that the claimant did not actually see or know that the finder found them. Rather, the finder admitted finding one purse, and the claimant then said, “According to your own words, you found two.” Rashi thus holds that this can constitute an admission of part. But there is an obvious difficulty. The finder is returning a lost object, and the Mishnah states that one who returns a lost object does not swear, as Rashi himself explains in several places. Had the finder remained silent the claimant would have had nothing. Rashi said what he did only in explaining Rabbi Yitzchak’s own statement. Rabbi Yitzchak does not accept the Mishnah’s exemption for a finder based upon the concern for tikkun olam, as is evident in the Gemara. Rashi therefore explained Rabbi Yitzchak correctly. According to the halakhah, however, we follow the Mishnah that a finder does not swear. Even in this case he should therefore not swear as a practical matter. If Rabbenu Yerucham copied Rashi’s explanation as a practical ruling, that appears difficult and requires study. What appears possible in defense of Rabbenu Yerucham is as follows. Rashi does not read the Gemara’s continuation with the text “this was also taught,” as Tosafot do. This raises the question: according to whom does Rabbi Yitzchak state his rule?

One must say that Rashi understands the final conclusion to depend upon the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Sages. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that a person does not brazenly deny the creditor’s son even though he did not receive the money directly from the son. If so, in a lost object case as well he would not brazenly retain the lost object for himself. His concept of brazenness follows Rabbenu Tam, who holds that it is considered brazenness even when the claimant cannot personally recognize the lie, as I explained at length in the rules of migo, simanim 112 and 113. We do not worry that perhaps the finder would simply refrain from picking up the object. Why should he not pick it up? It may belong to a non Jew, or it may belong to a Jew where the finder discovers that the owner had already despaired before he found it, in which case it belongs to the finder. Accordingly, for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov there is no concern for tikkun olam that imposing an oath will deter finders from returning lost property. Rabbi Yitzchak can therefore require an oath. The Sages, however, hold that a person can brazenly deny the creditor’s son because he did not receive the money directly from him. Certainly they would say the same of a lost object. There is therefore a real concern for tikkun olam, and the finder does not swear. According to this, if the claimant originally did not know that the defendant had borrowed from him, and the defendant himself admits the loan but says, “I repaid half,” after which the claimant says with certainty, “I know you did not repay me at all,” there is no tikkun olam concern according to anyone. The concern is not that a person will refrain from taking possession of the object in the first place, only that he might refrain from returning it. Here, withholding repayment is a direct act of brazenness. Although the claimant may not independently know the defendant’s falsehood, the defendant received the money directly from him. The principle that one may brazenly deny because he did not receive anything from the claimant applies only to a son, whereas here the original creditor himself gave the money. Everyone therefore agrees with Rabbi Yitzchak that the tikkun olam rationale does not exempt the defendant, and he must swear. This, in my view, is the best defense of Rabbenu Yerucham, though it still requires study. The Maharsha’s words in the second chapter of Ketubot also tend in this direction. He addresses the Maharshal’s question that the Mishnah could have taught, according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, that Rabbi Yehoshua concedes where the claimant had not first made a demand. The Maharsha answers that the case cannot be established where witnesses exist. At first glance this answer is difficult to understand. The proposed case is that the claimant made no demand and did not know that anything was owed to him. The defendant voluntarily admitted owing one hundred but claimed that he had repaid fifty. Necessarily, the claimant then says with certainty that the fifty was not repaid, because otherwise there would be no definite claim capable of generating an oath. If he now has a definite claim, the defendant’s only migo is that he could have remained silent and never admitted the debt. If witnesses establish the original loan, that migo indeed disappears, because the defendant cannot deny the loan, while the claimant directly denies repayment. This seems to explain the Maharsha’s answer. According to the approach above, however, the matter is clearer. If Rabbenu Yerucham is correct, then according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov the son is treated like the original creditor, because Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that even toward the son the defendant does not brazenly deny. Thus, if no claim was initially made and the claimant’s certainty arose only from the defendant’s admission, the defendant is still one who admits part and must swear. What then is the Maharshal’s question that the Mishnah should teach that Rabbi Yehoshua concedes and exempts him where the claim was not made first? Necessarily, after the voluntary admission the claimant would have to say with certainty that no repayment occurred. But in precisely that case, according to Rabbenu Yerucham’s reading of Rashi, a Torah oath applies. There is therefore no possible formulation in which Rabbi Yehoshua would concede exemption, and the Maharshal’s question would never arise. It appears, however, that the Maharsha follows those authorities who hold that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Sages disagree only where the son says, “I stood there and saw that you did not repay, because I never moved away from them,” or an equivalent claim based upon his own observation. If the son says only, “My father told me so,” then even Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agrees that the defendant can be brazen toward him. They derive this from the Gemara in Shevuot, where the first clause, “I owe your father one hundred and fed him half,” is exempt because the defendant is returning a lost object, and the Gemara establishes it as a case where the son did not make a fully independent definite claim. If the son’s claim were wholly uncertain, however, why would the Gemara need the reason that the defendant is returning a lost object? No oath is imposed on an uncertain claim in any event, as the Mordechai asks. One must therefore say that the son’s claim is definite in the sense that he says, “My father told me,” yet it is not based upon his own observation. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agrees that in such a case the defendant can be brazen toward the son. At the same time, the statement “my father told me” is sufficiently definite to support an oath where the other requirements exist, for otherwise the Gemara could simply have said that the claim itself is insufficient rather than invoking the lost object rationale. Accordingly, the Maharsha can distinguish two versions of the Maharshal’s proposed case. If the defendant voluntarily says, “I owe your father one hundred but repaid fifty,” and the son says, “I stood there and saw that you never repaid,” there is no question at all. According to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov the defendant must indeed swear, exactly as Rabbenu Yerucham maintains, so the Mishnah could not present this as a case in which Rabbi Yehoshua concedes exemption. If instead the son says only, “My father told me that you did not repay,” then even Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agrees that the defendant can brazenly deny him. In that setting there would be no oath because the defendant is returning a lost object, although absent that rationale the son’s statement is a definite claim. The Maharsha therefore correctly answers that such a case cannot be reconciled with the clause involving witnesses. If witnesses establish the loan, the defendant can still say that he repaid the entire amount to the father, because even according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov he can brazenly deny the son where the son did not personally observe the matter. Thus the witnesses would not produce the result stated in the Mishnah. The Maharsha’s words are therefore clear and compelling, and they assume Rabbenu Yerucham’s understanding of Rashi. The Rosh in Gittin writes that the Rif, who holds that Rabbi Yitzchak’s rule does not accord with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov after the Gemara concludes that a person can be brazen toward the son, does not follow Rashi’s explanation. Rashi maintains that even at the conclusion the case concerns an actual minor, because the lost object was handed over after the claimant had reached adulthood. This is difficult. What practical difference should the claimant’s actual age make? The Maharsha explicitly writes that even according to Rashi, Rabbi Yitzchak’s rule is not inherently tied to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. It seems that the Rosh understood that if the claimant is an adult, the case necessarily concerns one who claims with certainty based upon what his father told him, rather than one who personally stood and saw the event. Otherwise, why would the Gemara call him “a minor in his father’s matter”? If he personally saw everything, his claim is not dependent upon his father’s matter at all. He is called a minor in his father’s matter precisely because his knowledge rests upon his father’s statement. This also resolves another point. According to the view that the Sages agree that a defendant cannot brazenly deny the son where the son personally stood and saw, why does the Gemara establish the Mishnah in Shevuot concerning oaths to a minor specifically according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rather than the Sages, by saying that the son stood and saw? If the claimant is truly an adult, that would not fit the Mishnah’s designation “a minor in his father’s matter,” because his claim rests on his own observation. According to Rashi, however, the claimant is an actual minor. It is therefore entirely possible that he stood and saw and is still called a minor simply because of his age. The Rosh certainly understood the comparison stated above. If a defendant can brazenly deny the son, he can likewise brazenly retain a found object, creating the concern that an oath will deter him from returning it. If he cannot brazenly deny the son, there is no comparable concern regarding a found object. But where the son personally stood and saw, everyone agrees that the defendant cannot brazenly deny him, and the lost object case likewise concerns one who stood and saw, as the Maharshal and Rashba explain, such as where the claimant stood on his roof and saw the finder lift the object. Rashi can therefore compare the two cases because even with a son who personally observed the matter the defendant can be brazen if the son is an actual minor. According to Tosafot, however, the claimant is not an actual minor, and the phrase “minor in his father’s matter” must mean that his knowledge depends upon his father’s report. The lost object case, which involves direct observation, is therefore not comparable to the case of the son at all. Examine this carefully.

Here one page is missing from our master’s words. It is a loss to be regretted. When I was young I merited to draw living waters from the well of my maternal grandfather, our master the gaon, of blessed memory. I heard from him a small portion of these matters, and because they remain engraved in my memory I have copied them here so that his holy words should not be lost.

segments.he: אפי' היה שכרו פרוטה הש"ך סק"ב האריך בסתירת הרמב"ם דבפי"א מהלכות שכירות פ' דאפי' היה שכרו בפרוטה כמ"ש בש"ע כאן ואולם בפ"ג מטוען ונטען הביא דעה זו בשם רבותיו והוא פ' דצ"ל כפירה ב' כסף והדברים סותרים זא"ז ואף אם נדחוק ברמב"ם דלמעשה לא ביקש להורות נגד רבותיו ופ' אפי' בפרוטה ישבע או כמ"ש הגאון ח"צ בתשובה דרמב"ם מודה בשכיר דיטול פרוטה בשבועה רק נחלק עם רבותיו באינך נשבעים ונוטלים דמד"ת היו נוטלים בלי שבועה ובזו ס"ל לרמב"ם דלא החמירו כ"א בכפירה שתי כסף מה נאמר ונדבר בטור דמכריע בריש ס"ז כרמב"ם דבעי כפירה שני כסף בשכיר ודלא כהגאון מר"ץ ובסוף ס"ז כתב כלשון המוזכר בש"ע דאפי' היה שכרו פרוטה והש"ך כתב ליישב ותמצית לשונו שצריך כל מקום הנתבע שיכפור בב' מעין ואם לא כפר תחילה ב' מעין אין הב"ד פוסקים לו שבועה אלא צריך שיכפור ב' מעין ואז פוסקים לו הב"ד שבועה ואח"כ ישבע התובע כתקנת חז"ל ונוטל אף מפרוטה ומעלה עכ"ל והיא ז"ל לרוחב בינתו קיצר במובן וסמך עצמו אמבין כמותו ואולם אנחנו לא נדע כוונתו דאם כופר בשני מעין איך ישבע אח"כ אפי' מפרוטה ומעלה הא הכפירה היה שני כסף ואם מודה אח"כ דמתחילה שקר טען לתבוע שני מעין עד שפסקו עליו הב"ד שבועה כדינו ובאמת אין לו תביעה רק בפ"א ובזו נימא דהואיל דכבר פסקו הב"ד שבועה אף דעכשיו נתגלה דאין לו רק פ"א מ"מ הפסק שבועה עומד במקומו מלבד דזה דוחק לכוון בלשון הרמב"ם כנראה מדברי הרמב"ם וטור אף גם דברים אלו רחוקים מסברא דכיון דשורש הדין אם אינו תובע רק פרוטה ולא שתי כסף דאין לו דין נשבע ונוטל ולא תקנו חכז"ל בו התקנה א"כ וכי בשביל זה שכיחש בב"ד ותבע יותר מכפי הראוי כאשר פיו ענה בו יועיל ערמתו לישבע אפי' בפ"א אשר לא כדת ותקנות חז"ל ונמצא חוטא טוען שקר בב"ד נשכר ונקי אשר לא נשא לשוא נפשו לטעון שקר בב"ד אבד והפסיד דא"נ ואולי כוונת הש"ך דוודאי כפירה והכחשה ביניהם צריך להיות שתי כסף דומיא דש"ד במ"מ רק על דרך זה כגון השכיר תובע ב' כסף קצצת לי ותן לי אותם והלה מכחישו לא קצצתי לך אלא פ"א ונתתיו וא"כ ע"ז בכפירת הקציצה הבעה"ב נשבע ונפטר וא"כ אין השכיר נשבע ונוטל רק פ"א ובזה אמרי' דמ"מ ישבע כיון דעכ"פ הכפירה והכחשה יש כאן בשני כסף דאף דהוא אינו נוטל רק פ"א בשבועה מ"מ יש כאן כפירה כשיעור הנ"ל משא"כ אם מתחילה ועד סוף אין כאן כפירה והכחשה רק בפ"א ולא בב' כסף בזו ל"ת חז"ל לישבע כי לא תקנו רק דומיא דמ"מ וכעין נדון זו יש למצוא בכל נשבעין ונוטלים כגון נחבל עדים שמעידים על חבורה א' שראוהו שלם קודם הקטטה כדלקמן דבהא הנחבל נשבע ונוטל וחבלה זו אינו עולה יותר רק פ"א אמנם נחבל טוען עוד חבורה א' עשית בי וע"ז אין עדים שנכנס ת"י שלם ואין הנחבל נאמן וא"כ באמת יש כאן כפירה והכחשה ב' כסף כשנצרף שני החבורות אבל לענין נשבע ונוטל אין כאן רק פ"א דעל החבלה שניה א"נ ומ"מ נשבע הואיל ועכ"פ יש כאן כפירת שתי כסף אבל אם מעולם לא נתווכחו רק בחבלה א' שהוא רק שוה פרוטה בזו לא תקנו וכן י"ל בנגזל שראו עדים נכנס ולא היה התביעה רק בפרוטה רק הנגזל טוען עוד נכנס בלי ראית עדים ובצירוף שניהם יש כאן כפירות שתי כסף אבל מ"מ אין הנגזל נשבע ונוטל רק במה שראו עדים נכנס והוא רק שוה פ"א ובאמת יש מקום לסברא זו אבל ק' לכוונו בלשון טהור של הש"ך ואולי כוונתו דמתחילה כפר הבע"ב לשכיר בשני מעין ולבסוף הודה לו הבעל הבית שחייב לו ואינו מכחישו רק בפרוטה ואמרי' הואיל וכפר מתחילה והזקיקו השכיר לידי שבועה יהיה עונשו דאף עכשיו יהיה השכיר נוטל בשבועה אפי' פ"א דאלו מתחילה הודה לו היה נשכר שלא הי' מגיע לשכיר שבועה אבל הוא הואיל וכיחש והב"ד פסקו שבועה לא זזה ממקומה אך זה דוחק גדול כמש"ל ואין לשון הרמב"ם וטור מורי' כן כלל ומה שנ"ל בישוב דברי הרמב"ם הוא כך דודאי טענת הראב"ד חזקה מה יעשה העני זה שהשכיר עצמו בפרוטה וכי לא חשו חכמים לכדי חייו אלא ס"ל ודאי אם לא היה שכרו רק פ"א ויש כאן הכחשה בפרעון ודאי דנוטל בשבועה כקו' הראב"ד אבל אם שכרו הי' ביותר בשני מעין רק שאינם מחולקים בפחות משני מעין דעל הנשאר מודים זל"ז הבעה"ב ושכיר בזו כיון דשכירות היה ביותר רק המחלוקה הוא רק בפרוטה אזדא קושית הראב"ד דהרי זה כשארי תובעים ונתבעין דאם אין הכחשה ביניהם בסך שני כסף לא אחשביהו חז"ל לתקן שבועה ואף באלו נשבעים ונוטלים כך כיון דהעסק שביניהם היה ביותר ודבר זה ברור ונכון בסברא והכי דייק למאוד לשון הטור דמתחילה הסכים לרמב"ם ובס"ס זה כ' אפי' היה שכרו פרוטה ישבע ויטול שכרו פרוט' דייק ולא קאמר אפי' תביעתו פרוטה אלא ודאי דלא לפי תביעתו דנין דאם היה שכרו שני כסף ותביעתו רק פ"א אין כאן שבועה כהכרעת הרמב"ם ז"ל אבל בשכרו פרוטה תקנו חז"ל שבועה וכן המחבר בלשונו לשון זהב בש"ע שמר דברי הטור וכ' אפי' היה שכרו פרוטה ובזו י"ל שבועה אבל אם תביעתו רק פ"א ושכרו היה יותר מודה לדברי הרמב"ם וכן יש להור' כמ"ש הב"ח והש"ך כי יש לפסוק כרמב"ם היותו מקיל ובפרט כי הוא רק שבועת התקנה ואין לנו אלא מה שכל המחברים הקדמונים שווי' בו והבו דלא נוסיף עלה לבטל ד"ת ולקח בעליו ולא ישלם:
segments.en: Even if his wage was only a perutah. The Shach in seif katan 2 discusses at length an apparent contradiction in the Rambam. In chapter 11 of Hilkhot Sekhirut the Rambam rules that even if the worker’s wage was only a perutah, as the Shulchan Aruch rules here. Yet in chapter 3 of Hilkhot To’en VeNitan he cites in the name of his teachers the view that there must be a denial of two silver ma’ah, and his words there plainly imply that he accepts that requirement. The two rulings appear contradictory. Even if we strain to explain that the Rambam did not wish in practice to rule against his teachers and therefore wrote that even for a perutah the worker swears, or if we adopt the explanation of the Chacham Tzvi that the Rambam agrees regarding a hired worker that he may collect even a perutah with an oath, and disagrees with his teachers only regarding the other categories who swear and collect, who by Torah law would collect without an oath and concerning whom the Rambam holds that the Sages imposed their additional oath only when the denial is at least two silver ma’ah, what are we to say about the Tur? At the beginning of siman 87 the Tur rules like the Rambam that even regarding a hired worker there must be a denial of two silver ma’ah, contrary to the Chacham Tzvi’s approach, while at the end of that siman he writes in the very language cited here that even if the wage was only a perutah the worker swears and collects. The Shach attempts to reconcile this. The substance of his words is that in every case the defendant must initially deny two ma’ah. If he did not originally deny two ma’ah, beit din does not impose the oath. Once he has denied two ma’ah and beit din has ruled that an oath is required, the claimant then takes the rabbinically instituted oath and may collect even from a perutah upward. The Shach, with the breadth of his understanding, expressed himself briefly and relied upon readers of his own level. We, however, do not understand his precise intent. If the defendant denies two ma’ah, how can the claimant later swear and collect only a perutah? The denial itself was two ma’ah. Perhaps the Shach means that the claimant later admits that his original claim of two ma’ah was false and that in truth he has only a one perutah claim, but since beit din already ruled that he may swear, the ruling remains in force even after it becomes clear that the actual claim is only a perutah. This is exceedingly difficult to read into the Rambam and Tur. More fundamentally, it is remote from reason. If the root of the law is that one who claims only a perutah is not among those whom the Sages allowed to swear and collect, because the enactment was never made for such a small claim, how can the claimant benefit from having lied in beit din and exaggerated his claim until beit din imposed an oath? His deceit would then enable him to collect a perutah with an oath contrary to the enactment, so that the sinner who falsely inflated his claim profits while the innocent claimant who truthfully demanded only a perutah loses. That cannot be correct. Perhaps the Shach’s intent is different. The total denial and contradiction between the parties must indeed concern two silver ma’ah, analogous to the Torah oath of one who admits part of a claim, but the amount ultimately collected under the special oath may be only a perutah. For example, the worker claims, “You fixed my wage at two silver ma’ah and you owe them to me.” The employer says, “I fixed your wage at only one perutah, and I already paid that perutah.” Concerning the amount of the wage, the parties contradict one another regarding two silver ma’ah. The employer swears regarding the wage amount and is thereby exempt from the larger claim. The worker then has only the one perutah which even the employer admitted was the agreed wage, and he may swear and collect that perutah. Thus, although the amount collected through the worker’s oath is only a perutah, the dispute itself involved the requisite two silver ma’ah. The same pattern can be found in the other categories who swear and collect. In the case of an injured person, for example, witnesses may establish one injury by testifying that they saw him whole before the quarrel, so that with respect to that injury the injured party may swear and collect. Suppose that injury is worth only one perutah, but the injured party also claims a second injury worth enough that the two injuries together equal two silver ma’ah. As to the second injury there are no witnesses who saw him enter the other’s domain uninjured, so he is not believed under the special enactment. There is nevertheless a total denial of two silver ma’ah when both injuries are counted, while the amount he may actually recover by oath is only the single perutah injury. Similarly, in the case of one who was robbed, witnesses may have seen the defendant enter the claimant’s premises in circumstances supporting a claim worth only one perutah, while the claimant alleges another entry not seen by witnesses. Together the denials reach two silver ma’ah, yet the special oath permits recovery only for the one perutah transaction witnessed by the witnesses. There is room for such a distinction. It is nevertheless difficult to fit it into the Shach’s precise language. Perhaps instead he means that the employer initially denied two ma’ah and thereby caused beit din to impose the worker’s oath, but later the employer admitted all but one perutah. Since his initial denial generated the oath, his punishment is that even after narrowing the dispute to one perutah the worker may still swear and collect. Had he admitted the larger part from the beginning, he would have benefited by avoiding the special oath. Since he falsely denied more and beit din already imposed the oath, it remains in place. This, however, is also very strained, as explained above, and the wording of the Rambam and Tur does not indicate it. What appears to me to resolve the Rambam is as follows. The Raavad’s objection is powerful: what is a poor laborer to do if he hired himself out for only a perutah? Did the Sages not care for his livelihood merely because the wage was small? Certainly, if the entire wage was only a perutah and the dispute concerns whether that perutah was paid, the worker swears and collects, as the Raavad argues. But if the worker was hired for a larger amount, at least two silver ma’ah, and the parties agree about all but one perutah, so that their actual dispute concerns only that perutah, the Raavad’s concern no longer applies. This worker’s employment was substantial, like an ordinary monetary transaction, and the parties differ only over a very small residual amount. In such a case, just as with ordinary claimants and defendants, the Sages did not consider a denial below two silver ma’ah significant enough to support the special oath. The same should apply to all who swear and collect. Since the underlying transaction was larger, but their actual dispute concerns only one perutah, the enactment does not apply. This distinction is clear and sound. The Tur’s wording is especially precise. Earlier he accepted the Rambam’s rule requiring a denial of two silver ma’ah. At the end of the siman he writes, “Even if his wage was a perutah, he swears and collects his wage.” He carefully says “his wage was a perutah,” not “his claim was a perutah.” The legal test is therefore not merely the amount currently demanded. If his entire wage was two silver ma’ah but his present disputed claim is only one perutah, there is no oath, in accordance with the Rambam’s rule. If the original wage itself was only one perutah, however, the Sages did institute the worker’s oath even for that small amount. The Mechaber likewise preserves this golden precision in the Shulchan Aruch by writing, “Even if his wage was a perutah.” He too agrees that if the original wage was larger and only a perutah remains disputed, the Rambam’s minimum applies. This is therefore how one should rule, as the Bach and the Shach conclude, for the Rambam’s view is the more lenient one. Moreover, we are dealing only with an oath created by enactment. We should extend such an enactment no further than the points on which the early authorities agree.

en_segments: Even if his wage was only a perutah. The Shach in seif katan 2 discusses at length an apparent contradiction in the Rambam. In chapter 11 of Hilkhot Sekhirut the Rambam rules that even if the worker’s wage was only a perutah, as the Shulchan Aruch rules here. Yet in chapter 3 of Hilkhot To’en VeNitan he cites in the name of his teachers the view that there must be a denial of two silver ma’ah, and his words there plainly imply that he accepts that requirement. The two rulings appear contradictory. Even if we strain to explain that the Rambam did not wish in practice to rule against his teachers and therefore wrote that even for a perutah the worker swears, or if we adopt the explanation of the Chacham Tzvi that the Rambam agrees regarding a hired worker that he may collect even a perutah with an oath, and disagrees with his teachers only regarding the other categories who swear and collect, who by Torah law would collect without an oath and concerning whom the Rambam holds that the Sages imposed their additional oath only when the denial is at least two silver ma’ah, what are we to say about the Tur? At the beginning of siman 87 the Tur rules like the Rambam that even regarding a hired worker there must be a denial of two silver ma’ah, contrary to the Chacham Tzvi’s approach, while at the end of that siman he writes in the very language cited here that even if the wage was only a perutah the worker swears and collects. The Shach attempts to reconcile this. The substance of his words is that in every case the defendant must initially deny two ma’ah. If he did not originally deny two ma’ah, beit din does not impose the oath. Once he has denied two ma’ah and beit din has ruled that an oath is required, the claimant then takes the rabbinically instituted oath and may collect even from a perutah upward. The Shach, with the breadth of his understanding, expressed himself briefly and relied upon readers of his own level. We, however, do not understand his precise intent. If the defendant denies two ma’ah, how can the claimant later swear and collect only a perutah? The denial itself was two ma’ah. Perhaps the Shach means that the claimant later admits that his original claim of two ma’ah was false and that in truth he has only a one perutah claim, but since beit din already ruled that he may swear, the ruling remains in force even after it becomes clear that the actual claim is only a perutah. If the root of the law is that one who claims only a perutah is not among those whom the Sages allowed to swear and collect, because the enactment was never made for such a small claim, how can the claimant benefit from having lied in beit din and exaggerated his claim until beit din imposed an oath? segments.he: ושעש' עמו מלאכ' דאם לא יעידו עדים גם ע"ז לא מהני עדותן על ששכרו דהא נאמן במגו דאי בעי אמר לא בא לעשות מלאכתו:
segments.en: And that he performed work for him.

segments.he: מתוך שיכול לומר לא שכרתיך כו'. ואף על גב דמטעם שמתוך שהוא טרוד בפועליו אמרי' דשכח וסבר שפרעו ומ"ה אמרו דישבע השכיר ולא משום דחשדינן לי' במשקר במזיד וא"כ לא שייך מגו בכה"ג דאטו משום מיגו יזכור טפי מ"מ כיון שהב"ה טוען ברי לי שלא שכחתי ויודע אני שפרעתיו אין לנו להחזיקו במשקר לומר שאינו ברי לו והוא משום כיון דיש לו מגו דאי בעי לשקר בהאי. דאמר ברי לי הי' משקר לו' לא שכרתיהו כלל משא"כ כשאין לו מיגו דאמרי' דמסופק הוא ומשקר לטענת ברי כ"כ התו' ועפ"ר:
segments.en: Since he could have said, 'I did not hire you,' etc. Although the reason the Sages say that the worker swears is that the employer is preoccupied with his workers and may have forgotten and thought that he paid him, not because we suspect him of deliberately lying, and if so a migo should seemingly not apply, since how would a migo make him remember better, nevertheless the employer claims with certainty, 'I did not forget; I know that I paid him.' We therefore do not presume that he is lying about the certainty of his own recollection, because he has a migo: if he wished to lie while making a definite claim, he could have lied by saying, 'I never hired him at all.' When he has no such migo, however, we say that he is actually uncertain and falsely presents his claim as certain. So wrote Tosafos. See the Prisha.

segments.he: ואם מוד' מקצת ישבע שבועת התור'. כ"כ הרמב"ם והטור הסכים עמו ולא כר"י והטור הביאו דכתב דבמוד' הב"ה במקצתו אינו נאמן במיגו דלא שכרתיך דה"ל מיגו דהעזה ועפ"ר:
segments.en: If witnesses do not also testify that the worker actually performed the work, testimony merely that he hired him does not help, because the employer has a migo that he could have said the worker never came to perform the job.Since he could have said, 'I never hired you,' etc.

segments.he: וכן אם תבעו אחר זמנו כו'. הטעם דחזק' הוא דאין הפועל משהה שכירתו לאחר זמנו אם לא שתבעו בזמנו ולא נתנו לו וכמ"ש ואזיל ולא כע"ש שכ' ז"ל שבתוך זמנו הב"ה טרוד בתשלומי פועליו ולקיים מצות ביומו תתן שכרו אבל לאחר זמנו אינו טרוד בפועליו ולפי דבריו אם הבע"ה אמר אחר זמנו שפרעו תוך זמנו לא הי' נאמן הבע"ה כיון שאז הי' טרוד וז"א כדאי' בגמ' ועד"ר:
segments.en: Although the reason Chazal shifted the oath to the worker is that the employer is preoccupied with his workers and may have forgotten whether he paid, rather than because we suspect deliberate lying, the migo still has relevance to the legal structure of the claim.

segments.he: שכיר יום כל הליל' זה יתבאר לקמן בטור ובדברי המחבר סי' של"ט בס"ד:
segments.en: The worker's special oath is a rabbinic enactment created in a defined setting.

segments.he: שתבעו כל זמנו. כן הוא לשון הגמ' והרמב"ם ול"ד קאמר שתבעו הרב' פעמים אלא כוונתו שכל זמנו הי' בתביע' ובחזק' שלא פרע והיינו שתבעו בעדים בסוף זמנו והשיב לו שיבא אח"כ והרי שמעו שלא פרע לו תוך זמנו בזה השכיר נאמן לישבע וליטול עונה אחת אחר סוף זמנו כן מוכח פירושו מדברי הרא"ש והטור שהם כתבו על מ"ש בגמ' שתובעו כל זמנו שתובעו בסוף זמנו ולא כמ"ש בע"ש שכ' ז"ל ואם יש לו עדים שהי' תובעו כל ליל שלישי כלומר שהי' יוצא ונכנס לתובעו תמיד כל הליל' של יום שלישי כו' וכן כפל ושלש ל' זה וז"א אלא כמ"ש:
segments.en: Where the employer has an alternative claim that would have exempted him and the evidentiary conditions of the enactment are not established, the claimant cannot extend the enactment beyond its stated case.

segments.he: הרי זה נשבע ונוטל כל אותו יום כו'. עד הרי זה נשבע ונוטל כל יום חמישי עפ"ר ודריש' שם כתבתי והוכחתי מל' הרמב"ם והטור דכוונת הרמב"ם הוא דלעולם נותנין לו זמן לישבע וליטול בזמן התביע' ומ"ה אם תבעו בליל התחלת יום ג' לחוד אין נותנין לו אלא יומו דיום ג' דהיינו י"ב שעות נגד י"ב שעות דזמן התביע' ואם תבעו ליל ג' וגם יום ג' ולא פרעו אזי נותנין לו זמן כל יום ד' לילו ויומו כאורך זמן התביע' והרמב"ם כ' תחל' דאף אחר התביע' הראשונ' אם לא הית' אלא ליל א' אין נותנין לו יותר מזמן ליל' ואח"כ אשמועינן רבותא דאפי' אחר זמן ראשון אם יש עדים שחזר ותובעו בליל ד' ויומו דנותנין לו כנגדו כל יום ה' ליל' ויומו להיות נאמן לישבע וליטול ואע"ג דעבר הבע"ה זמן פרעון גם כל יום ג' וה"ל ליתן לו נגדם ב' ימים ולילות די"ל כיון דלעת הערב ביום ג' לא תבעו נמצא כשכלה היום ג' הי' בחזקת פרוע ואע"ג דכשחזר בתחלת ליל ד' נותנין זמן אלא נגדו עמ"ש בפריש' עוד מילתא בטעמא ואיך הוכחתי זה ודו"ק:
segments.en: Thus witnesses must establish both the hiring and the work, and then the special worker's oath applies concerning payment.
