segments.he: והיינו דוקא כלי וכו' עיין מש"ל בזה בסעיף י"ד ע"ש בס"ק י"ב:
segments.en: And we were like a vessel and so on, and so on, we shall see it as a result of it:

segments.he: אבל אם משכנו המלוה שאר דברים וכו' יש להבין מאין הוציא רמ"א דין זה כי מה שנרשם תשובת רשב"א מה שכתב ב"י דכ' דקיימא לן בתמורה לכ"ע אי עבד מהני היינו היכי דהתורה נתקו לעשה השב תשיבם וכן ברי"ו לא כתב רק אי תפס תפס אבל בדברים שאין בהם החזרה אם כן לא קאי עלה השב תשיבם ואם כן הדרן לכללא אי עביד לא מהני. דהא לא שייך עלי' השב תשיבם. ואולי סברת הרשב"א דאם כן לימא איכא בינייהו בדברים שאין צורך להחזירם לרבא צריך להחזיר ולאביי א"צ להחזיר ומדלא משני הכי ש"מ דהכל בכלל אי עביד מהני והיינו כיון דחזינן דהתורה אמרה בדברים שיש בו צורך להחזיר דמהני מעשיו וא"צ להחזיר רק בעת הצורך ש"מ דדעת התורה דבזה יהיו מעשיו קיימים ואם כן מיני' במקום שא"צ להחזיר דגם כן מעשיו קיימים דהא חזינן דגילוי דעת התורה דבזה הלאו מה דעביד יהי' מהני ואם כן בכל דבר בזה הלאו אפילו בדבר שאין בהם צורך החזרה אהני מעשיו:
segments.en: But if the creditor took other items as collateral, etc. It requires explanation where the Rama derived this rule. The Rashba responsum cited by the Beit Yosef says that we rule in Temurah that according to everyone an unlawful act is effective where the Torah itself connected the prohibition to a positive command, "you shall surely return it." Rabbenu Yerucham likewise says only that if the creditor seized the item, the seizure is effective. But with respect to items to which the duty of return does not apply, the positive command of return is absent. We should then return to the general rule that an act done in violation of the Torah is ineffective. Why should the collateral acquisition stand? Perhaps the Rashba's reasoning is as follows. Otherwise, the Gemara could have identified a practical difference between Abaye and Rava in the case of collateral that does not require periodic return. According to Rava, the creditor would have to return it because the unlawful taking is ineffective, while according to Abaye he would not. Since the Gemara does not give this distinction, it follows that the creditor's acquisition is effective in all forms of collateral. Once the Torah reveals, with respect to items that must be returned when needed, that the original taking is effective and the creditor need return the item only at the appropriate times, Scripture thereby reveals its intention that conduct violating this particular prohibition can nevertheless create a valid pledge. We may therefore infer that even where there is no periodic duty of return, the creditor's acquisition remains effective. Now. The Rambam likewise indicates that the creditor does not receive lashes. The Mishneh LaMelech asks why.

segments.he: והנה ברמב"ם מבואר ג"כ דאין לוקה וע"ז תמה המשנה למלך למה הלא בחבל עשיר למה לא ילקה הא לא ניתק לעשה דאין בו מצות החזרה ול"ל הואיל ולאו ניתק לעשה במצוה שיש בו החזרה אם כן תו ליכא בי' מלקות כלל דנהפוך הוא דרמב"ם כתב יחיד שעושה תמורה לוקה ולא ניתק לעשה דכתיב והי' הוא ותמורתו קודש הואיל וציבור לא ניתק לעשה דציבור הממירים אין תמורת' קודש והרי להיפוך דאם בצד א' לאו לא ניתק לעשה אף בדבר דניתק לעשה לוקה. ובאמת מה שהקשה מעשיר היה מקום ליישב דנראה אם בשעה שחבל היה עשיר ואח"כ נעשה הלוה עני חייב להחזיר סוף כל סוף עכשיו הרי נצרך למשכון והיא שמלתו לעורו במה יכסה וכן לפי דברי ר"ש דאמר אלמנה עשירה ממשכנין אבל לא עני' דמשיאה שם רע בשכוני' אם היתה בשעת משכון עשירה ואחר כך עני' אין חייב להחזיר דעדיין יש הוצא' שם רע בשכוני' וזהו דברי תוספתא והוא בירושלמי ג"כ רש"א אלמנה עני' אין ממשכנין אבל עשירה ממשכנין ואין מחזירין לה מפני שמשיאה שם רע בשכנותה והדבר תמוה לכאורה בעשירה בלא"ה אין מחזירין כדכתיב ואם עני הוא וכו' ומה צורך טעם שמשיא' שם רע וכו' אבל לפמ"ש ניחא דמיירי אם אחר כך ירדה מנכסים מ"מ אין מחזירין דא"כ חזר הדבר להשיאה שם רע בשכנותיה וזהו כוונתו עשירה ממשכנין ואין מחזירין ר"ל אם העני אחר כך. ולפ"ז לק"מ דאף בעשיר הרי בגדר ניתק לעשה דכל שעה הרי עומד להחזיר קאי אם יעני ואם כן הרי עליו חיוב השבה והרי בכלל ניתק לעשה משא"כ בתמורה בציבור שהמירו שא"א לעול' לבוא לכלל ניתק לעשה דבציבור לעולם אין תמורתו קודש שפיר אמרינן דלא הוי ניתק לעשה ולק"מ. אך אין זה מספיק בחובל דברים שאין בהם תורת תזרה כגון חבל אוכל נפש גופי' ואם כן בהו לא שיך ניתק לעשה ואם כן הקושי' במקומו הוה ליה לרמב"ם לפרש דלוקה בהו עכ"פ. ולכן צריך לומר בקושי' משנה למלך דיש לחלק בין ניתק לעשה לניתק לעשה דודאי ניתק לעשה דהוא ממילא שפיר אמרינן כמו בתמורה לחומרא דהואיל דבציבור ליתא אף ביחיד לוקה ולא קשה איך יתכן לומר לו קום ועשה וילקה דהא אין אנו צריכין למעשהו דממילא הוא ותמורתו קודש וקדשהו שמים. אבל במקום דצריך לומר קום ועשה אם כן א"א לומר דילקה דלא יתכן לומר לו קום ועשה ולהלקותו וע"כ דאין בלאו זה מלקות ואם כן אמרינן להיפוך אף גבי מקום דאין בו קום עשה אין בו מלקות דאין לחלק הלאו לחצאין או כולו מלקות או כולו פטור ולכן כאן היכא דאמרינן קום החזיר אי אפשר להלקותו ואם כן בכל דבריהם אין כאן מלקות אף במקום דלא שייך קום עשה וסברא הלזו לחלק בין ניתק לעשה דתמורה לשאר ניתק לעשה כתבו תוס' חולין דף פ"א ד"ה הנח וכו' דכתבו דהך דתמורה לא הוי ניתק גמור דבלאו מעשיו יהי' הוא ותמורתו קודש ע"ש והדברים נכונים כמ"ש אבל עכ"פ מ"ש דאם העשיר והעני דמחויב להחזיר אמת כמ"ש בירושלמי:
segments.en: If the creditor takes collateral from a wealthy debtor, the positive command to return the pledge when needed does not presently apply, so why is the prohibition considered one redirected to a positive command? It is not enough to say that because the same prohibition is redirected to a positive command in cases involving a poor debtor, it is never punishable by lashes. The Rambam rules concerning substitution of sacred property that an individual who makes a temurah receives lashes, even though Scripture says that both the original and its substitute become sacred. The Rambam's reason is that when a congregation makes a substitution, the substitute does not become sacred, so in that setting the prohibition is not redirected to a positive command. Thus, where one application of a prohibition is not redirected to a positive command, lashes can still apply even in another application where a positive consequence exists. That appears to be the reverse of what would be needed here. The Mishneh LaMelech's question from the case of a wealthy debtor can be answered. If the debtor was wealthy when the collateral was taken but later became poor, the creditor must then return the item when needed. Ultimately, it is now the debtor's garment for his skin, with what else will he sleep? Conversely, according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one may take collateral from a wealthy widow but not from a poor widow because returning the pledge repeatedly could give her a bad reputation among her neighbors, if she was wealthy when the collateral was taken and later became poor, the creditor still does not return it, because the repeated visits would now create that same bad reputation. This is the meaning of the Tosefta, also cited in the Yerushalmi: Rabbi Shimon says that one may not take collateral from a poor widow, but may take it from a wealthy widow and does not return it to her because doing so could give her a bad reputation among her neighbors. At first glance this is puzzling. A wealthy debtor is not entitled to periodic return in any event, as the verse says, "and if he is a poor man." Why does Rabbi Shimon need the additional reason of a bad reputation? According to what was explained, the Tosefta means that even if the wealthy widow later becomes poor, the creditor still does not return the pledge, because repeated returns would then create the very bad reputation the Torah sought to avoid. Thus "one may take from a wealthy widow and does not return it" means even if she later becomes poor. Accordingly, there is no difficulty from the wealthy debtor. Even while he is wealthy, the prohibition remains within the category of a prohibition redirected to a positive command, because the collateral is constantly subject to a potential future obligation of return if the debtor becomes poor. By contrast, where a congregation makes a substitution, there is no possibility that the act will ever become subject to the positive consequence that the substitute becomes sacred, because a communal substitution never takes effect. In that case the prohibition is genuinely not redirected to a positive command. This answer does not suffice, however, for collateral that is itself excluded from the law of return, such as implements used to prepare food, if one unlawfully took them. There the positive command of return does not apply at all, so the Rambam should at least have explained that lashes are administered in such cases. The Mishneh LaMelech's basic difficulty therefore remains. It seems that one must distinguish between two kinds of prohibitions redirected to a positive command. Where the positive consequence occurs automatically, as with temurah, there is room to say stringently that because in one application the prohibition is not redirected to a positive command, lashes remain possible even in the application where the positive consequence occurs. There is no contradiction in both effects applying, because no one must tell the offender to perform an act. The original and substitute are automatically sacred through Heaven's decree. Where, however, the positive command requires beit din to tell the offender, "Arise and do this," it is impossible to administer lashes while simultaneously directing him to perform the corrective act. The prohibition therefore cannot carry lashes in the cases where the positive command applies. Once the Torah framed the prohibition in that manner, we do not divide a single prohibition into halves by imposing lashes in some applications where the corrective command happens not to apply. Either the prohibition as a whole is one for which lashes are imposed, or it is not. Here, because in its ordinary application we direct the creditor to return the collateral, lashes are excluded from the prohibition as a whole, even in an instance where no actual command to return applies. Tosafot in Chullin 81a, in the passage beginning "leave it," make this distinction between the rule of temurah and an ordinary prohibition redirected to a positive command. They write that temurah is not a complete example of such a prohibition because the sanctity of the substitute takes effect without any corrective act by the offender. Their reasoning accords with what was explained. In any event, the point stated above is correct: if the debtor was wealthy and later became poor, the creditor must return the collateral at the times of need, as appears from the Yerushalmi.

en_segments: And we were like a vessel and so on, and so on, we shall see it as a result of it:

But if the creditor took other items as collateral, etc. It requires explanation where the Rama derived this rule. The Rashba responsum cited by the Beit Yosef says that we rule in Temurah that according to everyone an unlawful act is effective where the Torah itself connected the prohibition to a positive command, "you shall surely return it." Rabbenu Yerucham likewise says only that if the creditor seized the item, the seizure is effective. But with respect to items to which the duty of return does not apply, the positive command of return is absent. We should then return to the general rule that an act done in violation of the Torah is ineffective. Why should the collateral acquisition stand? Perhaps the Rashba's reasoning is as follows. Otherwise, the Gemara could have identified a practical difference between Abaye and Rava in the case of collateral that does not require periodic return. According to Rava, the creditor would have to return it because the unlawful taking is ineffective, while according to Abaye he would not. Since the Gemara does not give this distinction, it follows that the creditor's acquisition is effective in all forms of collateral. Once the Torah reveals, with respect to items that must be returned when needed, that the original taking is effective and the creditor need return the item only at the appropriate times, Scripture thereby reveals its intention that conduct violating this particular prohibition can nevertheless create a valid pledge. We may therefore infer that even where there is no periodic duty of return, the creditor's acquisition remains effective. Now. The Rambam likewise indicates that the creditor does not receive lashes. The Mishneh LaMelech asks why.

If the creditor takes collateral from a wealthy debtor, the positive command to return the pledge when needed does not presently apply, so why is the prohibition considered one redirected to a positive command? It is not enough to say that because the same prohibition is redirected to a positive command in cases involving a poor debtor, it is never punishable by lashes. The Rambam rules concerning substitution of sacred property that an individual who makes a temurah receives lashes, even though Scripture says that both the original and its substitute become sacred. The Rambam's reason is that when a congregation makes a substitution, the substitute does not become sacred, so in that setting the prohibition is not redirected to a positive command. Thus, where one application of a prohibition is not redirected to a positive command, lashes can still apply even in another application where a positive consequence exists. That appears to be the reverse of what would be needed here. The Mishneh LaMelech's question from the case of a wealthy debtor can be answered. If the debtor was wealthy when the collateral was taken but later became poor, the creditor must then return the item when needed. Ultimately, it is now the debtor's garment for his skin, with what else will he sleep? Conversely, according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one may take collateral from a wealthy widow but not from a poor widow because returning the pledge repeatedly could give her a bad reputation among her neighbors, if she was wealthy when the collateral was taken and later became poor, the creditor still does not return it, because the repeated visits would now create that same bad reputation. This is the meaning of the Tosefta, also cited in the Yerushalmi: Rabbi Shimon says that one may not take collateral from a poor widow, but may take it from a wealthy widow and does not return it to her because doing so could give her a bad reputation among her neighbors. At first glance this is puzzling. A wealthy debtor is not entitled to periodic return in any event, as the verse says, "and if he is a poor man." Why does Rabbi Shimon need the additional reason of a bad reputation? According to what was explained, the Tosefta means that even if the wealthy widow later becomes poor, the creditor still does not return the pledge, because repeated returns would then create the very bad reputation the Torah sought to avoid. Thus "one may take from a wealthy widow and does not return it" means even if she later becomes poor. Accordingly, there is no difficulty from the wealthy debtor. Even while he is wealthy, the prohibition remains within the category of a prohibition redirected to a positive command, because the collateral is constantly subject to a potential future obligation of return if the debtor becomes poor. By contrast, where a congregation makes a substitution, there is no possibility that the act will ever become subject to the positive consequence that the substitute becomes sacred, because a communal substitution never takes effect. In that case the prohibition is genuinely not redirected to a positive command. This answer does not suffice, however, for collateral that is itself excluded from the law of return, such as implements used to prepare food, if one unlawfully took them. There the positive command of return does not apply at all, so the Rambam should at least have explained that lashes are administered in such cases. The Mishneh LaMelech's basic difficulty therefore remains. It seems that one must distinguish between two kinds of prohibitions redirected to a positive command. Where the positive consequence occurs automatically, as with temurah, there is room to say stringently that because in one application the prohibition is not redirected to a positive command, lashes remain possible even in the application where the positive consequence occurs. There is no contradiction in both effects applying, because no one must tell the offender to perform an act. The original and substitute are automatically sacred through Heaven's decree. Where, however, the positive command requires beit din to tell the offender, "Arise and do this," it is impossible to administer lashes while simultaneously directing him to perform the corrective act. The prohibition therefore cannot carry lashes in the cases where the positive command applies. Once the Torah framed the prohibition in that manner, we do not divide a single prohibition into halves by imposing lashes in some applications where the corrective command happens not to apply. Either the prohibition as a whole is one for which lashes are imposed, or it is not. Here, because in its ordinary application we direct the creditor to return the collateral, lashes are excluded from the prohibition as a whole, even in an instance where no actual command to return applies. Tosafot in Chullin 81a, in the passage beginning "leave it," make this distinction between the rule of temurah and an ordinary prohibition redirected to a positive command. They write that temurah is not a complete example of such a prohibition because the sanctity of the substitute takes effect without any corrective act by the offender. Their reasoning accords with what was explained. In any event, the point stated above is correct: if the debtor was wealthy and later became poor, the creditor must return the collateral at the times of need, as appears from the Yerushalmi.

segments.he: מסדרין לב"ח כו'. ילפינן מיכה מיכה מערכין ועפ"ר:
segments.en: We arrange necessities for a creditor's debtor, etc. This is learned by a verbal analogy from the laws of valuations.

segments.he: ונותנין לו מהכל מזון כו'. פי' כשיש לו מזונות בביתו נותנין לו ממנו על ל' יום והמותר למלו' ואם אין לו מזונות בביתו מוכרים קצת מטלטלים כדי שיתנו לו דמי מזונות על ל' יום וכמ"ש המחבר בסכ"ז:
segments.en: They give him food from everything for thirty days, etc. If he has food in his house, they leave him enough for thirty days and the remainder goes to the creditor. If he has no food, some movable property is sold to provide him the money for thirty days' food, as stated in seif 27.

segments.he: אע"פ שאכל תחלה כעני. שמתחל' צמצם נפשו כדי לפרנס מהמותר לבני ביתו משא"כ עתה שאין נותנין להן כלום א"צ להרעיב נפשו בשביל המלו' וה"ה איפכא אם הי' אוכל תחלה כעשיר ממעטין עכשיו ממה שרגיל בו וכדמסיק בכסות ועפ"ר שם כתבתי דמשמעות ל' הרמב"ם והביאו הטור והמחבר בר"ס צ"ט שכ' שנותנין מזון כדרכו כו' לא משמע קצת הכי וצריכין לדחוק ולפרש כדרכו כפי הראוי להיות דרכו דהיינו כמו בינוני שהוא דרך המיצוע וראוי לבני אדם לנהג בו ע"פ דרכם והנהגת':
segments.en: Even if until now he ate as a poor person. Until now he may have restricted himself so that the surplus could support his family. Now, since nothing is set aside for them, he need not starve himself for the creditor. Conversely, if he formerly ate as a wealthy person, his standard is reduced now to an intermediate level. Rambam's expression, "food according to his manner," must therefore be understood as the manner properly fitting him, namely the moderate middle path.

segments.he: אלא מעבירין אותו ממנו. פי' ל"מ שאין נותנין לו מעות להלביש נפשו בבגדים הללו אלא אפי' היו עליו בגדים הללו לוקחין אותן מידו:
segments.en: Rather, they remove it from him. Not only do they refrain from giving him money to clothe himself in such expensive garments; even if he is currently wearing them, they take them from him.

segments.he: ושאר צרכי המט'. פי' כרים וכסתות וסדינין ובשע' שהי' ממשכן אותו לא הניח בידו אלא מפץ ומצע וכרים היו נוטלים מידו ביום ומחזירים לו בלילה וכמ"ש המחבר בסי"ז אבל עתה שבא לסדר לו ולמכור המותר מסדרים לו גם כרים וסדינים ומניחין אותן בידו:
segments.en: And other bedding needs. This means pillows, cushions, and sheets. When merely taking collateral they leave him only a mat and bedding, while pillows are taken during the day and returned at night. But when arranging his needs before selling the remainder, they also leave pillows and sheets in his possession.

segments.he: לאשתו ולבניו כו'. דכתיב ואם מך הוא מערכך ע"פ אשר תשיג יד הנודר ודרשינן על פי זה שיש לו מסדרין לו ומדכ' הוא דרשינן תחייהו מערכך לו ולא לאשתו ובניו ועפ"ר מ"ש עוד מזה:
segments.en: Not for his wife and children, etc. From the verse regarding valuations, "according to what the hand of the one making the vow can attain," Chazal derive that the arrangement is made for him alone, not for his wife and children.

segments.he: ואין לוקחין לו כלים מדמי המרובה. פי' למין המועט שבידו אין מוכרין מהמרובה למלאות המועט דה"א דיכול לומר עד השתא דהיה בידי ממין אחד הרבה כלים והייתי משאיל לשכיני מאותו מין והן השאילו לי מהמין השני שאין בידי ממני כדי צרכי משא"כ עתה שלוקחין מידי ממין המרובה היתר מכדי צרכי קמ"ל ועפ"ר:
segments.en: They do not purchase lacking utensils from the proceeds of excess utensils. If he has more utensils of one type than he needs and too few of another type, they do not sell the excess to fill the deficiency. One might have argued that until now he lent his excess utensils to neighbors and borrowed from them the type he lacked, and once the excess is taken away he can no longer do so. The ruling teaches otherwise.

segments.he: לא צמדו ולא חמורו. צמדו פי' הבקרים שהוא חורש בהן דומיא דחמורו ועפ"ר:
segments.en: Not his yoke nor his donkey. "His yoke" means the oxen with which he plows, analogous to his donkey.

segments.he: אין מניחין לו ספריו. והא דמניחין לו תפילין לפי שהוא דרך מלבוש ומצוה שבגופו טור:
segments.en: They do not leave him his books. Tefillin are left because they are worn as clothing and are a personal mitzvah.

segments.he: ומ"ש ואפי' ספר תורה. אף דכתב הרא"ש דבזמן הזה המצוה טפי בקניית ספרים מבספר תורה כמו שכ' הטור יורה דעה בשמו בריש הלכות ספר תורה הטעם שבזמנינו מעמידין הספר תורה בהיכל ואין למדין מתוכו ע"ש י"ל דלשון בע"ת בשם ר"י מברצלוני נקט ואזיל הטור והמחבר וגם המחבר לטעמיה אזיל שכתב שם בי"ד שלא בא הרא"ש אלא ללמדינו שגם קניית שאר ספרים מצווים אנו בה ושעכ"פ בקניית ס"ת מצות עשה במקומה עומדת ע"ש:
segments.en: Even a Torah scroll is taken. Although the Rosh writes that nowadays buying other holy books is an even more practical mitzvah than owning a Torah scroll, since Torah scrolls are kept in the ark and not used for ordinary study, the Tur and Mechaber quote the older formulation. The Mechaber himself holds that the Rosh meant only to add that buying other books is also a mitzvah, not to uproot the positive mitzvah of acquiring a Torah scroll.

segments.he: מתנה ע"מ להחזיר וכו' עיין אורים מ"ש בשם בעה"ת אך נראה כל זה הוא למ"ד דאין הבדל בין שבועה דלהבא ושבועה דלעבר אבל לפי דפסק הש"ע לעיל סי' פ"ז דיש הבדל א"כ בלא"ה לק"מ דאם יש מתנה ע"מ להחזיר והוא נשבע שאין לו אם כן בשעת שבועה מוציא שקר מפיו וחמירא ליה משא"כ אם לא ישבע רק כשירוויח שיתן לו ואח"כ ירויח הרי לא יצאה שבועה לשקר מפיו קילא ליה. ואין להקשות א"כ כשנשבע להבא למה לא יוכל להשביעו כל שלשים יום הרי כשנשבע כל ל' יום הרי חמירא ליה דהוי שבועה לעבר ויוצא שקר מפיו דהך שבועה בלא"ה חומרת הגאונים ולא החמירו בו אף דקילא ליה וזהו להטיל עליו שבועה בכוון מחדש בזו אמרינן בתקנתא דגאונים אין להחמיר כ"כ אבל מתחילת שבועה דבלא"ה נשבע כל שאנו יכולים לכלול בתוך שבועה דחמירא ליה ולא יקל ראשו בשבועה עבדינן ולכך כללינן בשבועה דלא החביא ולא נתן מתנה ע"מ להחזיר וזה פשוט ונכון:
segments.en: A gift on condition that it be returned, etc. See Urim for what I wrote in the name of Baal HaTerumot. That discussion is necessary according to the view that there is no meaningful distinction between an oath concerning the future and an oath concerning the past. According to the Shulchan Aruch's ruling above in siman 87 that the two are different, the matter is simpler. If a debtor presently possesses property given to him on condition that it be returned and swears, "I have nothing," he utters a falsehood at the moment of the oath. Such an oath is especially severe. By contrast, if he merely swears that whatever he later earns he will pay to the creditor, and he subsequently earns money and fails to pay, the oath was not false when spoken. His later violation is less severe in that respect. One might ask that if an oath about future payment is lighter, why not require the debtor to renew it every thirty days? At the time of each renewed oath, if he already possesses assets, the oath would concern a present fact and be more severe. The answer is that this entire oath is itself an added stringency instituted by the Geonim. They did not impose repeated new oaths every thirty days merely to increase pressure. But when the debtor is already taking the original required oath, we include within it every relevant present matter that can make him take the oath seriously. Therefore he swears that he has not hidden assets and has not transferred them as a gift on condition of return. This is simple and correct.

segments.he: נראה וכו' עיין אורים מ"ש בשם המ"מ דא"נ לומר דחייב לאחרים וכתב המ"מ דמזה מוכח דסבירא ליה לרמב"ם מלוה ע"פ מוקדם ומלוה בשטר מאוחר מלוה על פה קודם דאם לא כן מה קנוניא יש דנהי דהאמת אתו מ"מ הא מלוה בשטר קוד' וכ' הש"ך דאין כאן הוכחה דמיירי במטלטלין או נכסים שקנה אחר הלואת שניהם ובשטר לא נכתב דאקני ואם כן אלו האמת שחייב בעל פה גם כן היה הדין יחלוקו ולכך כתב הרמב"ם דא"נ מפני קנוני'. ואין דבריו ברורים כי בדבר שאין בו דין קדימה אם חייב לאחד מימים ימימה ובא היום לפני עדים ועושה לאחר שטר אחר שחייב לו טרם שגבה הראשון בב"ד הרי כל דברים הנ"ל שאין בהם דין קדימה יחלוקו בין שני חובות הללו וזה פשוט ואם כן המודה בב"ד שחייב לאחר בעל פה לא זו דיש לו מגו דאם רצונו לקנוני' הקצרה ידו לכתוב שט"ח בעדים שבעצם היום הזה נתחייב מנה לפלוני והרי כאן שני חובות שוי' ליטול בנכסי' ההם אף גם דמה שהודה בב"ד שחייב לפלוני מעת הודאה משוי' ליה חוב דלו יהיה דאינו חייב לו כלל מ"מ מתחייב בהודאתו בפני עדים כמש"ל בסי' מ' ומכ"ש המודה בפני ב"ד דמשעת הודאה הוי ליה לחוב גמור ואם כן עדיין מטלטלין ודכוותי' יחלוקו דהא יש כאן ב' חובות ואין נ"מ בקדימה ואיחור ועכצ"ל דמיירי הרמב"ם מנכסים שיש בהן קדימה ולכך לולי דאינו נאמן היה מלוה ע"פ קודם לגבות וזה פשוט וברור:
segments.en: It appears, etc. See Urim for what I wrote in the name of the Maggid Mishneh, that the debtor is not believed to say that he owes money to others. The Maggid Mishneh writes that from this ruling it follows that the Rambam holds that an earlier oral loan has priority over a later documented loan. Otherwise, what collusion is there? Even if the debtor's statement were true and he owed the earlier oral debt, the later documented creditor would still collect first. The Shach rejects the proof. He says the case may involve movable property, or property acquired only after both loans where the documented instrument did not contain an after-acquired-property clause. In such property there is no priority, so if the alleged oral debt were genuine the two creditors would divide. The Rambam therefore says the debtor is not believed because of the concern for collusion. This is not clear. In property where priority does not matter, suppose the debtor truly owes one creditor from long ago, and today, before that creditor collected through beit din, the debtor appears before witnesses and executes a new document acknowledging that he owes another person a separate debt. The two claims would divide that property. That is obvious. Accordingly, when the debtor appears before beit din and says that he owes another person an oral debt, he has an obvious migo if his goal is collusion. He could simply execute a valid debt instrument before witnesses today in favor of that person, thereby creating a second debt that unquestionably shares equally in property to which no priority applies. Moreover, even without an underlying debt, a formal admission before beit din that he owes the person money can itself create a binding obligation from the time of the admission, as explained above in siman 40. Certainly an admission before beit din produces a complete present debt. Thus, with respect to movable property and other assets in which earlier and later debts have equal rank, there would be no reason to disbelieve the debtor's statement on account of collusion. He can accomplish the same result openly and validly without the disputed assertion. The Rambam must therefore be speaking of property where priority matters. In that setting, if the debtor were believed, the alleged earlier oral creditor would collect before the later documented creditor. This confirms the Maggid Mishneh's proof and is clear.

segments.he: קודם שנשבע דעת הב"ח דאם אמר אז שמוחזקין בו דלית לי' נכסים דחייב לאחר נאמן כי מה קנוני' יש לו הא לית ליה והש"ך השיגו דלמא יש לו ואומר לקנוני' ואני לא הבנתי דבריו דהא אין מוחזקים בו דאית לי' רק דחושש הש"ך אולי יש לו בהסתר אם כן הא יש לו מגו דיהיב לאותו פלוני נכסים אלו דיש לו בהחבא ונחנו לא נדע והש"ך גופי' כתב ס"ק ו' באומר שחייב לאחר ויש לו מגו דיהיב לי' נאמן במגו וכאן כיון דאנו אין יודעים אם יש לו נכסי' הרי יכול ליתן נכסיו דיש לו בהחבא לאותו גבר ויש לו מגו ברורה ואין לומר דאולי אין רצונו להטמין מטמוניות או לתת לאחר פן יודע סודו ולכך מתחבל לומר דחייב לאחר דאם כן הא דפריך בגמ' פ' חזקת בראובן שמכר שדה שלא באחריות דא"י להעיד דמעמיד' בפני ב"ח ופריך הגמרא בממ"נ אי דאית ליה עליה דידי' הדר ואי דל"ל מה נ"מ וקשה מה קושי' דלמא יש לו מטמונים וחושש פן בין היום ומחר לאחר זמן יתגלה סודו ויטרוף הימנו ב"ח ולכך מתחבל שיהיה שדה זו קיים לגבות ב"ח ואם אח"כ יתגלה סודו מה שעבר עבר כי הלוקח היה שלא באחריות. אלא ודאי כיון דהוא בחזקת דלית ליה לא חיישינן דאית לי' במטמונים ומכ"ש בנדון הנ"ל דנשבע דלית ליה תו לא חיישינן למידי ודברי הב"ח ברורים:
segments.en: Before he swore. The Bach holds that if, at a time when the debtor is presumed to have no assets, he says that he owes money to someone else, he is believed. There is no apparent collusion, because according to the known facts he has nothing to distribute. The Shach disagrees, arguing that perhaps the debtor secretly owns assets and falsely claims another debt in order to protect them. I do not understand this. We do not presently know of any such assets. If the Shach merely fears that the debtor possesses hidden property, then the debtor has a clear migo. He could simply transfer those concealed assets to the alleged creditor without our knowledge. The Shach himself writes in seif katan 6 that where a debtor says that he owes another person money and has a migo that he could have given that person the assets, he is believed. Here, because we do not know that any assets exist, any hidden assets could be transferred directly. The migo is complete. One cannot answer that perhaps the debtor is unwilling to move or transfer the hidden property because he fears the secret will be discovered, and therefore prefers the false claim of debt. The Gemara in Bava Batra, chapter Chazakat HaBatim, disproves such speculation. There it discusses Reuven who sold land without responsibility and cannot testify concerning the land because he may wish to preserve it for his own creditor. The Gemara asks: if he has other property, the creditor can recover from him; if he has none, what difference does it make to him whether this field remains available? According to the Shach's concern, the Gemara's question would fail. Perhaps Reuven has secret assets and fears that sooner or later they will be discovered, allowing his creditor to collect from him. He therefore prefers that the sold field remain available for the creditor. If the hidden assets are later discovered, the earlier sale was without responsibility and the buyer has no claim against him. The Gemara nevertheless does not entertain such a possibility. Evidently, once a person is presumed to lack property, we do not invent the possibility of secret assets merely to create a suspicion of collusion. All the more so here, after the debtor has actually sworn that he has nothing. The Bach's ruling is therefore clear.

segments.he: וי"ח בזה דעת הד"מ דהרשב"א בתשובה דכתב דאם נתן לאחיו בכת"י דחצי נכסיו הוא שלו ואח"כ יצא עליו כתוב' אשה וכתב הרשב"א דל"ל לקנוני' דהא אם ירצה יכול לתת לאחיו נכסיו במתנה עכ"ל ומזה הוכיח הד"מ דסבירא ליה דאף במקום חזקה כל מה שהוא ברשות אדם הוא שלו מ"מ אמרינן מגו וכן הוכיח מתשובת הרא"ש דפסק ביש לו עסקא בידו דנאמן לומר של פלוני הם במגו דיהיב ליה וע"כ כתב כאן דיש חולקים והרב הש"ך האריך לומר דל"ל בדעת רשב"א בזה דרשב"א גופי' כתב בתשובה דה"ל מגו במקו' חזקה וכדי שלא יהיה סתירה בדבריו צ"ל דשם היה נכסי' בחזקת וברשות אחיו ואם כן ליכא מגו במקום חזקה כלל וכן הרא"ש מיירי בידוע דיש לו עסקא מאחרים בידו ואם כן תו לא שייך חזקה כל מה שהוא ביד אדם הוא שלו ולכך ס"ל להרא"ש דמהימן במגו אבל זולת זה לא ודעת הש"ך דליכא כאן מחלוקת כלל וכולי עלמא ס"ל דלא אמרינן מגו במקום חזקה כזו ע"ש:
segments.en: Some disagree with this, which is the view of the Darkei Moshe. The Rashba writes in a responsum about a person who gave his brother a handwritten document stating that half of his property belonged to the brother, after which a woman's ketubah claim was presented against him. The Rashba says that we need not suspect collusion, because if he wished he could simply have given the property to his brother as a gift. From this the Darkei Moshe infers that even against the chazakah that property in a person's possession belongs to him, a migo can be accepted. The Darkei Moshe also brings support from a responsum of the Rosh, who rules that where a person holds investment property for another, he is believed to say that the property belongs to that other person because he could have given it to him. The Rama therefore writes here that some authorities disagree with the view rejecting such a migo. The Shach argues at length that the Rashba should not be interpreted this way. The Rashba himself elsewhere writes that such a migo is a migo against a chazakah. To avoid contradiction, the Shach says that in the first responsum the assets were actually in the brother's possession, so there was no chazakah that they belonged to the debtor. Likewise, the Rosh's case involved property known to have been received as investment property from others, so the ordinary chazakah that everything in a person's possession is his never arose. The Shach therefore concludes that there is no real dispute: all authorities agree that a migo cannot overcome this chazakah.

segments.he: ולא נראים דבריו כי אמת דברי רשב"א סותרים ויש לישבם ודלא כמ"ש הש"ך כי זהו דוחק לומר דמיירי דנכסים ברשות אחיו כי לא נזכר זה בתשובה הנ"ל רק הואיל ויש ביד אחיו כת"י מוקדם בזמן כי חצי הנכסים שייכים לו רק כל החשש אולי עשה קנוניא וכתב עכשיו הכת"י והקדים הזמן זהו בלא"ה חששא רחוקה לחוש לכה"ג במקום דלא נפל ולא איתרע וכמ"ש מהר"ם מלובלין עיין לעיל ס"ס מ"ג מ"ש שם. וא"כ בצירוף מגו דאי בעי יהיב לו אמרינן ולא שייך במקום חזקה כי כת"י שבידו מגרע חזקה שלו דכתבו בידו מקדם ומכח מגו אמרינן דאין כאן קנוניא. ולק"מ וכן בדברי הרא"ש יפה כתב הש"ך אבל מ"מ יפה כתב הרמ"א דיש חולקים כי רבים ס"ל דאמרינן מגו במקום חזקה. דהא כתבו התוס' ב"ב דף נ"א ע"ב ד"ה קבל כו' דביש בידו פקדון מאשה והוא מעות טמונים דלכ"ע זכה בהן הבעל כדין נכסי מלוג לאכול פירות ולירושה אם אמרה האשה של פלוני הם נאמנת במגו דאי בעי שקליה ויהיב ליה זולת אם אמרה בשעת מיתה דא"א למשקל כו' אז אינה נאמנת ולכך תניא יעשה פי' לפירושה וכ"כ הרא"ש וכ"פ בש"ע א"ע סימן פ"ו ע"ש וקשה הא נכסים בחזקתה של אשה שהן שלה בתורת נ"מ ואיך תהיה נאמנת במגו נגד חזקה להפקיע זכות בעל וביותר לפמ"ש הרמ"א בא"ע שם וכן דעת הסמ"ע לעי' סי' ס"ב ועיי' מ"ש שם דאפילו אשה הנו"נ בתוך הבית נאמנת במגו אף דהוא בחזקת שלה ושל בעלה ואין לדחות הואיל הוא מופקד ביד אחר דמ"ש הואיל והופקד מן האשה הרי זה כאלו הן בידה וכמ"ש הבית שמואל להדיא סי' פ"ו ע"ש ופשוט הוא. אלא שאני תמה המ"מ הביא הך סברא בשם הרמב"ן כי הוא היה כמסתפק אם לא נימא דהוי מגו במקום חזקה וכו' ואולם הרמב"ן גופיה כתב בחדושיו למס' ב"ב בפרק חזקת בשמעתא הנ"ל דאין האשה נאמנת לומר על נכסים שבידה שניתן לה במתנה מאחר ע"מ שאין לבעלה רשות בו כלל. דאי ס"ד דנאמנת א"כ למה קתני באומרת של אחרים היא אינה נאמנת למה הא יש לה מגו דאמרה שלי הוא וניתן לי ע"מ שאין לבעלי רשות בו. וכ"כ המ"מ בשמו פ' כ"ב מהל' אישות ע"ש וקשה הא הוי מגו במקום חזקה דכל מה שיש ביד האשה שלה הם יהיה באיזה אופן שיהיה עכ"פ שלה הם ומה מגו איכא דיהבי לאחר הא הוי מגו במקום חזקה. ומה ראיה יש מזה דלא מהימנת דשל אחר הוא ועכצ"ל דהמ"מ גופיה כתבו כמסתפק בשם הרמב"ן אי נימא דהוי מגו במקום חזקה ואין ספק זה מוציא מידי ודאי כמ"ש בחדושיו להדיא דאמרינן מגו כזו וצ"ע. וכן יש ראיה מהא דאמרינן בגמרא פ' זה בורר והביאו הרי"ף והרמב"ם בפ"י מהל' זכיה באומר ראיתי אביכם שהיה מטמין מעות ואמר של פלוני הם אינו נאמן ואם הם במקום שהמגיד היה יכול ליטלם נאמן במגו דהיה רוצה נוטלם ונותנם לפלוני ועיין לקמן סימן רנ"ה ס"ח ע"ש וקשה הא הוי במקום חזקה דחזקה מה שהיה ברשות אדם הוא שלו וסתמא איירי אפילו הטמנה הוא ברשות המצווה וכמ"ש הרא"ש בתשובה כלל ס"ח דין ב' ע"ש להדיא. ודוחק לומר דהואיל דהך דראה שהטמין היה יכול ללקחו מתחילה א"כ הרי המטמין הימנהו תחילה ודינו כשליש ונאמן בכל דבר דמ"ש דהא אף בנדון הש"ע הא המלוה האמין ללוה מתחילה ועד סוף דהרי היה יכול להבריח נכסיו כרצונו ומ"מ לא מהני מגו להפקיע חזקה הנ"ל ואיך יהיה הרואה יותר נאמן והגע עצמך המטמין גופיה אלו אמר של אחר אינו נאמן והרואה שהטמין ושמעו מפיו יהיה נאמן ודוחק לחלק דבאחר לא חיישינן לקנוניא כולי האי כמ"ש הרמב"ן כפי מ"ש בשמו המ"מ דשכיח בלוה קנוני' משא"כ באדם אחר וכל זה דוחק. וא"כ במקום שיש חשש דאותו אחר יש לו צד נגיעה והנאה וקנוניא בו לא יהיה נאמן וסתמא נאמר בש"ס וכל הפוסקים. ולכן יותר מסתברא לדינא אמרינן מגו אף במקום חזקה כזו. וכ"כ הש"ך בשם הרב הגדול ר"א בן חיים ז"ל וכן דעת הרי"ף בתשובה הביאו הבעה"ת שער ב' ח"א דנאמן לומר של אחר הוא רק אותו אחר יטול בשבועה אלא שבעה"ת תמה וכתב דהוא ט"ס דלמה נאמן ושבועה זו מה טיבו ולק"מ דאיירי דיש ללוה מגו ולכך נאמן רק מ"מ הנכסים בחזקתו ואותו אחר נוטל נכסים מה שהם משועבדים לב"ח והוי ליה כנכסים משועבדים דמה לי משועבדים ללוקח או לב"ח מאוחר והוא טוען שהם שלו לא יטול אלא אחר שבועה ואע"ג דאית ליה ללוה מגו הא ס"ל מגו לפטור משבועה לא אמרינן והרי זה דומה למלוה על משכון דג"כ נאמן במגו דלקוח ומ"מ חייב שבועה דה"ל נוטל ולא אמרינן מגו לפטור משבועה ואף זה הרי זה ניטל מן ב"ח שקדמו ולא יטול אלא בשבועה ולא מהני מגו וכן נראה לדינא.
segments.en: But his explanation does not appear correct. It is true that the Rashba's responsa appear inconsistent, but they can be reconciled without the Shach's forced assumption that the property was physically in the brother's possession, a fact not stated in the responsum. The brother held an earlier handwritten acknowledgment that half the assets belonged to him. The only concern was that the debtor might have fabricated the document recently and antedated it in order to collude against the creditor. Even without a migo, that is a relatively remote suspicion where the document has not fallen, been impaired, or otherwise become suspect, as Maharam of Lublin explains. See what I wrote above at the end of siman 43. When the earlier document is combined with the migo that the debtor could have given the property away, we need not suspect collusion. The ordinary chazakah of ownership is already weakened by the prior document itself. The migo merely supports the conclusion that the document is genuine. There is therefore no contradiction in the Rashba. The Shach's explanation of the Rosh may be correct, but the Rama was nevertheless justified in saying that authorities dispute the broader principle. Many authorities accept a migo even against this kind of chazakah. Tosafot in Bava Batra 51b, in the passage beginning "he received," write that where money entrusted by a woman is hidden property that legally belongs to her husband as nichsei melog for purposes of fruits and inheritance, if she says that it belongs to a third person she is believed because she could simply take it and give it to that person. Only when she makes the statement at the time of death, when she can no longer practically take and transfer the money, does she lose credibility. The Rosh writes the same, and the Shulchan Aruch rules accordingly in Even HaEzer, siman 86. Yet those assets are presumptively hers as nichsei melog, with the husband's rights attached. How can her migo overcome that chazakah and remove the husband's rights? This is even stronger according to the Rama there and the Sema above in siman 62, who hold that even a wife who conducts business in the household is believed through such a migo although the property is presumptively hers and her husband's. One cannot distinguish merely because the property was deposited with a third party. Once it was deposited by the woman, it is legally treated as though it remained in her possession, as Beit Shmuel explicitly writes in siman 86. The proof therefore stands. I am also surprised by the attribution to Ramban. The Maggid Mishneh cites Ramban as uncertain whether such a migo should fail against the chazakah. Yet Ramban himself, in his novellae to Bava Batra in the same sugya, writes that a wife is not believed to say that property in her possession was given to her on condition that her husband have no rights in it. He proves this by saying that if she were believed, then when she says that the property belongs to another person she should likewise be believed through a migo that she could have claimed, "It is mine and was given to me on condition that my husband have no right in it." The Maggid Mishneh cites this in Ramban's name in Hilchot Ishut, chapter 22. But such a migo would itself appear to operate against the chazakah that property in a woman's possession belongs to her in the ordinary marital form, whatever the precise marital category may be. How can Ramban use it as an unquestioned migo if he definitively rejects migo against the chazakah? It seems that the Maggid Mishneh accurately described Ramban as only raising the concern as a possibility, while Ramban's own novellae show that he did not treat it as conclusive. A mere doubt cannot override an explicit proof from his own words. This requires study. There is further proof from the Gemara in Sanhedrin, chapter Zeh Borer, cited by the Rif and Rambam in Hilchot Zechiyah, chapter 10. If a person says, "I saw your father hiding money, and he said that it belonged to so-and-so," the witness is not believed. But if the money was hidden in a place from which the witness could himself have taken it, he is believed because he could have taken it and given it to that person. See below, siman 255, seif 8. Why is this not a migo against the chazakah that property in a person's possession belongs to him? The case can plainly involve money hidden on the deceased's own property, as the Rosh states explicitly in responsum rule 68, law 2. It is strained to answer that because the observer could have taken the money at the time of concealment, the owner thereby trusted him and gave him the legal status of a shalish, who is believed in his assertions. In the present case too, a creditor necessarily trusted the debtor with possession of his own assets and the debtor could have transferred them away, yet we do not automatically give him the evidentiary power of a shalish against the creditor. Indeed, it would be paradoxical if the person who hid the money himself would not be believed to say that it belonged to another, yet an observer who heard him say so would be believed. One could distinguish that collusion is more commonly suspected in a debtor than in a neutral third person, as Ramban may imply, but that too is strained. If the third party has a concrete interest in the outcome, the concern of collusion can arise as well, yet the Gemara and poskim state the rule generally. It therefore seems more correct as practical law that a migo can be accepted even against this kind of ownership chazakah. The Shach cites the great Rabbi Eliyahu ibn Chaim as holding likewise. The Rif also supports this in a responsum cited by Baal HaTerumot, sha'ar 2, part 1. He rules that a debtor is believed to say that property belongs to another person, although that other person must take the property with an oath. Baal HaTerumot is surprised and suggests a textual error: why should the debtor be believed, and what is the purpose of the other person's oath? There is no difficulty. The debtor has a migo that he could have transferred the assets, and is therefore believed. Nevertheless, the property is presently in the debtor's possession and is subject to the earlier creditor's claim. The alleged owner is now taking property away from that creditor. He therefore resembles one collecting from encumbered property. Whether the property was transferred to a purchaser or is claimed by a later creditor or owner, the person removing it from the earlier creditor should not collect without an oath. The debtor's migo does not eliminate that oath, because according to this approach we do not say that a migo exempts a claimant from an oath. This resembles a creditor holding a pledge who is believed through a migo of purchase regarding the amount of his claim, yet still must swear because he is collecting. The same applies here. The Rif's responsum is therefore coherent and supports the practical conclusion stated above.

segments.he: אם ידוע שיש לו עסקא מאחרים כו' דעת הש"ך דידוע בעדים ושהוא תוך זמנו שודאי שלא פרעו כלל דאל"כ הא נוכל לטעון דהחזיר לו העסקא והא דבעי נאמנות דידיה דאל"כ אמרינן דהך עסקא הוציא ואינו בעין ודבריו דחוקים ולא ידעתי מה צווך לזה הא יש לו מנו דיהיב לו וא"כ אף באומר שלא היה מחזיר העסקא היה נאמן במגו רק כל ריעותא דמגו דה"ל במקום חזקה דחזקה כל מה שהוא ברשות אדם הוא שלו וזהו באין ידוע דיש בידו משל אחרים אבל בידוע הא אזלא חזקה די דהא רגיל להיות בידו משל החרים וה"ל כמו סרסור דלא אמרינן ביה חזקה זו ויש לו מגו מעליא ונאמן שהוא של עסקא ולא היה מחזיר לו כלל וכלל וזה פשוט ובריר:
segments.en: If it is known that he has investment funds belonging to others, etc. The Shach understands this to mean that witnesses establish the existence of the investment and that it is still within its term, so that it is certain the debtor has not returned it. Otherwise, we could claim that he may already have returned the investment. According to the Shach, the debtor's own credibility is needed because without his statement we would say that he already spent the investment funds and they are no longer extant. His words are strained. There is no need for these additional conditions. The debtor has a migo that he could simply give the property to the investor. Even if he said that he had not returned the investment, he could be believed through that migo. The only weakness ordinarily affecting this migo is that it stands against the chazakah that whatever property is in a person's possession belongs to him. But where it is already known that he regularly holds investment property belonging to others, that chazakah no longer applies in the same force. His possession is comparable to that of a broker, for whom we do not presume that everything in his hands is his own. He therefore has a proper migo and is believed that the assets are investment property, without any need to establish that the investment has not yet been returned. This is simple and clear.

segments.he: מעסק פלוני הם וכתב הש"ך היינו להך פלגא דהוא פקדון אבל הנך פלגא דהיא מלוה יחלוקו עם ב"ח דמלוה להיצאה ניתנה כדקי"ל בסימן ק"ח דעסקא פלגא מלוה ודבריו תמוהים דהא מבואר בפ' המקבל דהך עסקא אינו נעשה מטלטלין אצל יתומים ופירש"י אפילו פלגא מלוה אין ליתומים בו ומכח זה הוציאו הרי"ף והרמב"ם והרא"ש הדין שם דאם יש עסקא ויש עליו בע"ח וכתובת אשה אין להם כלים בהך עסקא והיינו אפילו בפלגא מלוה כבואר שם בכל הפוסקים דהא השוו הך דינא דב"ח וכתובת אשה ליתומים וביתומים אמרו בכל עסקא וה"ה לגבי ב"ח וכן מבואר בי"ד סימן קע"ו ע"ש וזה פשוט דאין לב"ח כלים אפי' בהך פלגא מלוה. ואמת כי שם נזכר דאיכא עדים או שטר וברור דהך עסקא הוא של פלוני אבל מ"מ נלמוד דאין לב"ח זכות רפילו בהך פלגא מליה וא"כ כאן דיש לו מגו ונאמן היינו כמו עדים דמ"ש עדים ומ"ש מגו סוף כל סוף אתברר לגבי ב"ד דהך עסקא דיליה הוא ולית ליה ללוה חלק בו ואם כן פשיטא דאין לב"ח של לוה זכות בכל עסקא. ולא דמי כלל להך דסימן ק"ח דשם לא נודע אם החזיר או לא ולכן דברי הש"ך תמוהים עד למאוד:
segments.en: They are from the investment of so-and-so, and the Shach writes. The Shach says that this protects only the half of the investment that has the status of a deposit. The half legally treated as a loan must share with the debtor's other creditor, because loaned money is given for expenditure. This follows, he says, from the rule in siman 108 that an iska is half loan. His words are astonishing. The Gemara in the chapter HaMekabel explicitly states that investment property does not become ordinary movable property in the hands of the investor's heirs. Rashi explains that even the half treated as a loan does not become part of the heirs' ordinary assets. On this basis the Rif, Rambam, and Rosh derive the rule that if the investor holds an iska and also owes money to creditors or a wife's ketubah, those creditors have no claim against the investment property. This necessarily includes the loan half, as is clear from all the poskim there, because they equate the creditor and ketubah cases with the rule regarding heirs, and the Gemara speaks of the entire investment. The same is codified in Yoreh Deah, siman 176. It is true that those sources speak of a case established by witnesses or a document, so that it is certain the property is the investment of the other person. But once the debtor here has a valid migo and is believed, that evidentiary status is equivalent for this purpose to proof. What difference is there between witnesses and a migo once beit din accepts the fact that the property belongs to the investment? The debtor then has no beneficial ownership that his personal creditor can seize. This is entirely unlike siman 108, where it is uncertain whether the investment was already returned. Here the accepted fact is that the specific property presently held is the other person's investment. The debtor's creditor therefore has no right even in the half classified as a loan. The Shach's ruling is exceedingly difficult.

en_segments: A gift on condition that it be returned, etc. See Urim for what I wrote in the name of Baal HaTerumot. That discussion is necessary according to the view that there is no meaningful distinction between an oath concerning the future and an oath concerning the past. According to the Shulchan Aruch's ruling above in siman 87 that the two are different, the matter is simpler. If a debtor presently possesses property given to him on condition that it be returned and swears, "I have nothing," he utters a falsehood at the moment of the oath. Such an oath is especially severe. By contrast, if he merely swears that whatever he later earns he will pay to the creditor, and he subsequently earns money and fails to pay, the oath was not false when spoken. His later violation is less severe in that respect. One might ask that if an oath about future payment is lighter, why not require the debtor to renew it every thirty days? At the time of each renewed oath, if he already possesses assets, the oath would concern a present fact and be more severe. The answer is that this entire oath is itself an added stringency instituted by the Geonim. They did not impose repeated new oaths every thirty days merely to increase pressure. But when the debtor is already taking the original required oath, we include within it every relevant present matter that can make him take the oath seriously. Therefore he swears that he has not hidden assets and has not transferred them as a gift on condition of return. This is simple and correct.

It appears, etc. See Urim for what I wrote in the name of the Maggid Mishneh, that the debtor is not believed to say that he owes money to others. The Maggid Mishneh writes that from this ruling it follows that the Rambam holds that an earlier oral loan has priority over a later documented loan. Otherwise, what collusion is there? Even if the debtor's statement were true and he owed the earlier oral debt, the later documented creditor would still collect first. The Shach rejects the proof. He says the case may involve movable property, or property acquired only after both loans where the documented instrument did not contain an after-acquired-property clause. In such property there is no priority, so if the alleged oral debt were genuine the two creditors would divide. The Rambam therefore says the debtor is not believed because of the concern for collusion. This is not clear. In property where priority does not matter, suppose the debtor truly owes one creditor from long ago, and today, before that creditor collected through beit din, the debtor appears before witnesses and executes a new document acknowledging that he owes another person a separate debt. The two claims would divide that property. That is obvious. Accordingly, when the debtor appears before beit din and says that he owes another person an oral debt, he has an obvious migo if his goal is collusion. He could simply execute a valid debt instrument before witnesses today in favor of that person, thereby creating a second debt that unquestionably shares equally in property to which no priority applies. Moreover, even without an underlying debt, a formal admission before beit din that he owes the person money can itself create a binding obligation from the time of the admission, as explained above in siman 40. Certainly an admission before beit din produces a complete present debt. Thus, with respect to movable property and other assets in which earlier and later debts have equal rank, there would be no reason to disbelieve the debtor's statement on account of collusion. He can accomplish the same result openly and validly without the disputed assertion. The Rambam must therefore be speaking of property where priority matters. In that setting, if the debtor were believed, the alleged earlier oral creditor would collect before the later documented creditor. This confirms the Maggid Mishneh's proof and is clear.

Before he swore. The Bach holds that if, at a time when the debtor is presumed to have no assets, he says that he owes money to someone else, he is believed. There is no apparent collusion, because according to the known facts he has nothing to distribute. The Shach disagrees, arguing that perhaps the debtor secretly owns assets and falsely claims another debt in order to protect them. I do not understand this. We do not presently know of any such assets. If the Shach merely fears that the debtor possesses hidden property, then the debtor has a clear migo. He could simply transfer those concealed assets to the alleged creditor without our knowledge. The Shach himself writes in seif katan 6 that where a debtor says that he owes another person money and has a migo that he could have given that person the assets, he is believed. Here, because we do not know that any assets exist, any hidden assets could be transferred directly. The migo is complete. One cannot answer that perhaps the debtor is unwilling to move or transfer the hidden property because he fears the secret will be discovered, and therefore prefers the false claim of debt. The Gemara in Bava Batra, chapter Chazakat HaBatim, disproves such speculation. There it discusses Reuven who sold land without responsibility and cannot testify concerning the land because he may wish to preserve it for his own creditor. The Gemara asks: if he has other property, the creditor can recover from him; if he has none, what difference does it make to him whether this field remains available? According to the Shach's concern, the Gemara's question would fail. Perhaps Reuven has secret assets and fears that sooner or later they will be discovered, allowing his creditor to collect from him. He therefore prefers that the sold field remain available for the creditor. If the hidden assets are later discovered, the earlier sale was without responsibility and the buyer has no claim against him. The Gemara nevertheless does not entertain such a possibility. Evidently, once a person is presumed to lack property, we do not invent the possibility of secret assets merely to create a suspicion of collusion. All the more so here, after the debtor has actually sworn that he has nothing. The Bach's ruling is therefore clear.

Some disagree with this, which is the view of the Darkei Moshe. The Rashba writes in a responsum about a person who gave his brother a handwritten document stating that half of his property belonged to the brother, after which a woman's ketubah claim was presented against him. The Rashba says that we need not suspect collusion, because if he wished he could simply have given the property to his brother as a gift. From this the Darkei Moshe infers that even against the chazakah that property in a person's possession belongs to him, a migo can be accepted. The Darkei Moshe also brings support from a responsum of the Rosh, who rules that where a person holds investment property for another, he is believed to say that the property belongs to that other person because he could have given it to him. The Rama therefore writes here that some authorities disagree with the view rejecting such a migo. The Shach argues at length that the Rashba should not be interpreted this way. The Rashba himself elsewhere writes that such a migo is a migo against a chazakah. To avoid contradiction, the Shach says that in the first responsum the assets were actually in the brother's possession, so there was no chazakah that they belonged to the debtor. Likewise, the Rosh's case involved property known to have been received as investment property from others, so the ordinary chazakah that everything in a person's possession is his never arose. The Shach therefore concludes that there is no real dispute: all authorities agree that a migo cannot overcome this chazakah.

But his explanation does not appear correct. It is true that the Rashba's responsa appear inconsistent, but they can be reconciled without the Shach's forced assumption that the property was physically in the brother's possession, a fact not stated in the responsum. The brother held an earlier handwritten acknowledgment that half the assets belonged to him. The only concern was that the debtor might have fabricated the document recently and antedated it in order to collude against the creditor. Even without a migo, that is a relatively remote suspicion where the document has not fallen, been impaired, or otherwise become suspect, as Maharam of Lublin explains. See what I wrote above at the end of siman 43. When the earlier document is combined with the migo that the debtor could have given the property away, we need not suspect collusion. The ordinary chazakah of ownership is already weakened by the prior document itself. The migo merely supports the conclusion that the document is genuine. There is therefore no contradiction in the Rashba. The Shach's explanation of the Rosh may be correct, but the Rama was nevertheless justified in saying that authorities dispute the broader principle. Many authorities accept a migo even against this kind of chazakah. Tosafot in Bava Batra 51b, in the passage beginning "he received," write that where money entrusted by a woman is hidden property that legally belongs to her husband as nichsei melog for purposes of fruits and inheritance, if she says that it belongs to a third person she is believed because she could simply take it and give it to that person. Only when she makes the statement at the time of death, when she can no longer practically take and transfer the money, does she lose credibility. The Rosh writes the same, and the Shulchan Aruch rules accordingly in Even HaEzer, siman 86. Yet those assets are presumptively hers as nichsei melog, with the husband's rights attached. How can her migo overcome that chazakah and remove the husband's rights? This is even stronger according to the Rama there and the Sema above in siman 62, who hold that even a wife who conducts business in the household is believed through such a migo although the property is presumptively hers and her husband's. One cannot distinguish merely because the property was deposited with a third party. Once it was deposited by the woman, it is legally treated as though it remained in her possession, as Beit Shmuel explicitly writes in siman 86. The proof therefore stands. I am also surprised by the attribution to Ramban. The Maggid Mishneh cites Ramban as uncertain whether such a migo should fail against the chazakah. Yet Ramban himself, in his novellae to Bava Batra in the same sugya, writes that a wife is not believed to say that property in her possession was given to her on condition that her husband have no rights in it. He proves this by saying that if she were believed, then when she says that the property belongs to another person she should likewise be believed through a migo that she could have claimed, "It is mine and was given to me on condition that my husband have no right in it." The Maggid Mishneh cites this in Ramban's name in Hilchot Ishut, chapter 22. But such a migo would itself appear to operate against the chazakah that property in a woman's possession belongs to her in the ordinary marital form, whatever the precise marital category may be. How can Ramban use it as an unquestioned migo if he definitively rejects migo against the chazakah? It seems that the Maggid Mishneh accurately described Ramban as only raising the concern as a possibility, while Ramban's own novellae show that he did not treat it as conclusive. A mere doubt cannot override an explicit proof from his own words. This requires study. There is further proof from the Gemara in Sanhedrin, chapter Zeh Borer, cited by the Rif and Rambam in Hilchot Zechiyah, chapter 10. If a person says, "I saw your father hiding money, and he said that it belonged to so-and-so," the witness is not believed. But if the money was hidden in a place from which the witness could himself have taken it, he is believed because he could have taken it and given it to that person. See below, siman 255, seif 8. Why is this not a migo against the chazakah that property in a person's possession belongs to him? The case can plainly involve money hidden on the deceased's own property, as the Rosh states explicitly in responsum rule 68, law 2. It is strained to answer that because the observer could have taken the money at the time of concealment, the owner thereby trusted him and gave him the legal status of a shalish, who is believed in his assertions. In the present case too, a creditor necessarily trusted the debtor with possession of his own assets and the debtor could have transferred them away, yet we do not automatically give him the evidentiary power of a shalish against the creditor. Indeed, it would be paradoxical if the person who hid the money himself would not be believed to say that it belonged to another, yet an observer who heard him say so would be believed. One could distinguish that collusion is more commonly suspected in a debtor than in a neutral third person, as Ramban may imply, but that too is strained. If the third party has a concrete interest in the outcome, the concern of collusion can arise as well, yet the Gemara and poskim state the rule generally. It therefore seems more correct as practical law that a migo can be accepted even against this kind of ownership chazakah. The Shach cites the great Rabbi Eliyahu ibn Chaim as holding likewise. The Rif also supports this in a responsum cited by Baal HaTerumot, sha'ar 2, part 1. He rules that a debtor is believed to say that property belongs to another person, although that other person must take the property with an oath. Baal HaTerumot is surprised and suggests a textual error: why should the debtor be believed, and what is the purpose of the other person's oath? There is no difficulty. The debtor has a migo that he could have transferred the assets, and is therefore believed. Nevertheless, the property is presently in the debtor's possession and is subject to the earlier creditor's claim. The alleged owner is now taking property away from that creditor. He therefore resembles one collecting from encumbered property. Whether the property was transferred to a purchaser or is claimed by a later creditor or owner, the person removing it from the earlier creditor should not collect without an oath. The debtor's migo does not eliminate that oath, because according to this approach we do not say that a migo exempts a claimant from an oath. This resembles a creditor holding a pledge who is believed through a migo of purchase regarding the amount of his claim, yet still must swear because he is collecting. The same applies here. The Rif's responsum is therefore coherent and supports the practical conclusion stated above.

If it is known that he has investment funds belonging to others, etc. The Shach understands this to mean that witnesses establish the existence of the investment and that it is still within its term, so that it is certain the debtor has not returned it. Otherwise, we could claim that he may already have returned the investment. According to the Shach, the debtor's own credibility is needed because without his statement we would say that he already spent the investment funds and they are no longer extant. His words are strained. There is no need for these additional conditions. The debtor has a migo that he could simply give the property to the investor. Even if he said that he had not returned the investment, he could be believed through that migo. The only weakness ordinarily affecting this migo is that it stands against the chazakah that whatever property is in a person's possession belongs to him. But where it is already known that he regularly holds investment property belonging to others, that chazakah no longer applies in the same force. His possession is comparable to that of a broker, for whom we do not presume that everything in his hands is his own. He therefore has a proper migo and is believed that the assets are investment property, without any need to establish that the investment has not yet been returned. This is simple and clear.
