segments.he: מרצונו בלא ב"ד כו' בגמרא אמרינן אגבי' איהו בחוביה פליגי ר"א ורבינא אי הדרא אי לא וקיי"ל לא הדרא ופי' רש"י לא שמו ב"ד בע"כ של לוה וקם ליה מעצמו ולא הטריחו לדין ואמר לו טול קרקע זה בחובך עכ"ל ומזה יליף הרב ב"י דלא בא לב"ד כלל אבל בא לב"ד אע"ג דלבסוף נתרצה ליתן השדה כפי שומת ב"ד לא נקרא אגביה מעצמו והדרא וכי כתב הסמ"ע והש"ך השיג ודעתו אפילו נעשה שומא בב"ד רק לא הטריח לב"ד לעשות בע"כ והוא מעצמו נתרצה ואמר טול מ"מ פליגי ביה וקיי"ל דלא הדרא ואם כי לשון ברש"י משמע כהרב ב"י מ"מ לדינא נראה אם גבהו הלוה מעצמו בלי ב"ד כלל א"כ במה קניא המלוה להך שדה ע"כ בשטר מכירה כשאר מכירות דהא לא נעשה כאן שומת ב"ד ולא היה יד ב"ד באמצע כלל וא"כ מה טעמא דמ"ד דהדרא מה שומא יש כאן דנימא ביה הדרא הא לא היה שומא כלל וכל השדות אשר נמכרים הלוקח ודאי שאומד ושם אותו כמה שוה ואינו לוקח כסומא וכי בשביל זה יקרא שומא הלא לא היה שומת ב"ד כלל וכיון שהלוה נתן למלוה שטר מכירה מה איכפת ומאן מוכח אם מכרה לו בדמים מזומנים או מכרה בשביל שהי' לו חוב אצלו מקדם היינו מכירה גמורה ומה שומא הדרא שייך כאן וגדולה מזו דעת הריטב"א ב"מ אפילו בשומא בגבי' ב"ד ונתן לו שטר עבור זה לא מקרי תו שומא הדרא ומכ"ש באופן הלזה דלא נעשה מעולם בב"ד שום דבר והוא מכרו לו ונתן עליו שטר מכירה מי יבטלנו ואיך ס"ד לשום מ"ד דיהי' זה בגדר שומא הדרא וכמו כן אם נימא כדברי הש"ך דנעשית השומא בב"ד רק הכל היה מרצון הלוה דבא לב"ד שמו לזה והורידו אותו בתוך השדה כמ"ש רש"י בתחילת דבריו דלא היה בע"כ א"כ לישנא דגמרא דטעמא דמ"ד הדרא הא דלא אתא לב"ד משום כסופא לא יתיישב דהא הי' בב"ד ואם כי לא סירב וקיים כפי שב"ד של ישראל אומרים לו א"צ לטעם דכיסופא כך ראוי ויפה לו להיות כפוף לכל אשר יאמרו לו מבלי לסרב וכך מדת חכמים ונקיי דעת אלא נראה דמתחילה נעשה שומא בב"ד רק לבסוף קודם שטר הורד' מב"ד לא בא לב"ד והוריד בעצמו למלוה לתוך השדה ולכך איכא למ"ד דמ"מ הואיל ונעשית ע"י ב"ד הרי זו בכלל שומא הדרא וקיי"ל דלא הדרא הואיל דלא אטרח לב"ד ונעשה לבסוף כרצונו כמ"ש הש"ך ראיה משילם וכו' וזה ברור ונכון:
segments.en: Voluntarily, without beit din, etc. The Gemara says that where the debtor himself transferred land in payment of his debt, Rabbi Acha and Ravina dispute whether the appraisal returns, and we rule that it does not. Rashi explains that beit din did not appraise the land against the debtor's will. Rather, the debtor arose on his own, did not trouble the creditor to litigate, and said, "Take this land for your debt." From this the Beit Yosef infers that the case involves no beit din proceeding at all. If the parties had come to beit din and the debtor ultimately agreed to give the field at the court's valuation, it would still be treated as a judicial appraisal and would return. The Sema accepts this. The Shach disagrees and holds that even where beit din made the valuation, so long as the debtor did not force beit din to remove him against his will but voluntarily said to the creditor, "Take it," the dispute applies and practical law is that it does not return. Although Rashi's wording leans toward the Beit Yosef, practical logic favors a middle understanding. If the debtor transferred the land wholly outside beit din, how did the creditor acquire it? Presumably through an ordinary deed of sale or conveyance. There was no judicial appraisal at all. Every purchaser privately estimates the value of what he buys, yet no one calls that an appraisal subject to later reversal. If the debtor executed an ordinary deed transferring the land in satisfaction of a preexisting debt, that is a genuine sale. It is indistinguishable in form from a cash sale and there is little basis even for an opinion that the rule of reversible appraisal should apply. The Ritva goes farther and holds that even after judicial collection, if the creditor received an ordinary deed for the land, the appraisal no longer returns. All the more should a wholly private sale be final. On the other hand, the Shach's reading that the entire appraisal and placement occurred in beit din, with the debtor merely cooperating, does not fit the Gemara's explanation of the opinion that the appraisal returns because the debtor avoided beit din out of embarrassment. If he was already before beit din and simply obeyed their instruction without resistance, embarrassment is unnecessary. That is simply proper conduct for one who accepts a Jewish court's direction. The best explanation is therefore that the valuation was initially made through beit din, but before beit din issued the final writ or formally placed the creditor into possession, the debtor himself voluntarily placed the creditor into the field. One opinion says that because the process originated in beit din it remains a reversible appraisal. We rule that because the final transfer occurred voluntarily and without troubling beit din, it is treated like a voluntary disposition and does not return. This preserves both Rashi's language and the Shach's essential insight. However. A difficulty remains from the Rosh's discussion in Mi SheHayah Nasu'i concerning the mansion case.

segments.he: איברא דיש לדקדק א"כ בפ' מי שהי' נשוי בעובדא דאפדנא דהביא הרא"ש דעת רמ"ה ורבינו יונה דנתחבטו למה היה יוכל לעכב עליו מבלי להחזיר האפדנא הא קיי"ל שומא הדרא ומכח זה חידש ר"י דגבי לוקח לא אמרינן הדרא ומה קושי' דלמא שם הי' נעשה לבסוף הורדה הכל ברצון טוב מלוקח וא"כ קיי"ל דלא הדרא ולק"מ ודוחק לומר דא"כ רב אחא דס"ל הדרא הך פלוגתא דרמב"ח ורבא איך מתוקמי דהיו אמוראי קדמאי מיניה דזה דוחק. אמנם נראה כי יש לחלק בלוה גופיה דיכול ליתן קרקעות שלו מרצונו בפרעון חובו ודאי דאמרינן אם לבסוף נתן מעצמו היינו זבינא גמורה משא"כ בלוקח דאינו חייב למלוה כלל רק מכח שעבוד מוכרח ליתן למלוה והכל תלוי בב"ד כי אם תן מרצונו איך יחזור על המוכר והכל הוא בכח יד ב"ד כי הם הטורפים מלוקח ונותנים למלוה ולוקח לגבי מלוה מה עבידת' וא"כ לא שייך זה כלל ולכ"ע שומא הדרא דהכל בכח ב"ד יגבה ולא שייך כאן רצון כלל וצ"ע כי אף דמסתבר מ"מ לדינא צ"ע הואיל ולא נמצא כן במחברים:
segments.en: Ramah and Rabbenu Yonah struggle to explain why the creditor can prevent return of the mansion despite the general rule that an appraisal returns, and from there derive that an appraisal from a purchaser does not return. Why not simply answer that in that case the purchaser voluntarily allowed the final placement, making it nonreturnable under our rule? It is strained to say that those earlier amoraim necessarily followed the minority opinion in the later dispute. The distinction appears to be between the debtor and a purchaser. A debtor may voluntarily satisfy his personal obligation by giving his own land. When, after an appraisal, he chooses to hand it over without forcing beit din to complete the process, that voluntary act can become a genuine sale. A purchaser, however, owes the creditor nothing personally. The creditor reaches his land only by force of the preexisting lien and judicial seizure. If the purchaser simply hands over the land, he cannot later recover from his seller without a recognized judicial taking, and in substance the transfer remains dependent upon beit din. As between purchaser and creditor, therefore, there is no meaningful independent voluntary payment that would transform the seizure into an ordinary sale. Thus the Rosh's case remains a judicial appraisal and required the separate rule concerning purchasers. This distinction is persuasive, though because I have not found it stated by the authorities, practical law still requires study.

en_segments: Where land was appraised to a creditor, etc. The Ritva holds that if land was appraised to a minor, the appraisal is not reversed until the minor reaches adulthood and can convey the property back to the debtor. The Shach correctly explains that the Ritva must follow the authorities who regard reversal of an appraisal as requiring a new conveyance from creditor to debtor. According to Nimukei Yosef and those who hold that no new kinyan is required, the minor's incapacity to convey should make no difference and the appraisal could be reversed immediately. The Ritva indeed holds that a new kinyan is required, as appears in Shitah Mekubetzet. I have a different reservation. Many authorities compare the requirement to act uprightly and well that underlies reversal of an appraisal to the same principle underlying the law of bar metzra. Below, siman 175:47, we rule that where land is sold to a minor orphan, the adjoining owner has no bar metzra claim at all. Rivash siman 507 explains explicitly that the reason is not merely that no one is available to trouble on behalf of the minor, but that the command to act uprightly and well is not imposed in the same way upon a minor orphan. If so, the same reasoning should apply here. Since reversal of an appraisal rests entirely on that equitable principle, perhaps a minor should not be compelled to return the property at all. Practical law therefore requires study.

But an appraisal of movable property does not return, etc. Pilpula Charifta labors to explain why movable property differs from land, but the matter is simple. Movable property is commonly available for purchase. A person who receives money can ordinarily acquire equivalent movable goods elsewhere, so there is no special demand of upright and good conduct requiring return of the particular items formerly his. Land is different. Land is not commonly available, and a person naturally values his own land more than another's. The Sages therefore applied the principle of upright and good conduct and required reversal of a land appraisal. For that reason the Ritva considered whether unusually rare movable items might also be subject to reversal. He was pressed by the Gemara in HaMafkid, which asks whether Rav Nachman holds that appraisal returns based on his direction to return certain jewels to their owner. Since jewels are movable property, the Ritva suggested that rare movable items may differ. But most authorities explain that the Gemara's question was not from the jewels themselves. It was from Rav Nachman's accompanying rule concerning return of a mansion. Once that is the source, there is no need to distinguish among types of movable property. The Sages established one uniform rule: appraisal of movable property does not return.

He does not receive his expenses, etc. The Tur records a dispute whether the creditor whose appraised land is being redeemed is reimbursed for his expenditures. The Mechaber rules that because of the doubt money is not extracted from the debtor who is redeeming. The Sema objects that the creditor is lawfully in possession of the land, while the debtor removes him only by a rabbinic enactment. The creditor should therefore be considered the possessor, and the debtor should not recover the land until he satisfies the creditor's demand. At first glance the Mechaber has support from the Rosh in Bava Metzia, chapter HaMekabel. In the law of bar metzra, where the adjoining owner says that the seller reduced the price for everyone while the purchaser says that the reduction was personal to him, the Rosh places the burden of proof on the adjoining owner. The land belongs to the purchaser by strict law, and the adjoining owner's claim rests only on the rabbinic principle of upright and good conduct. The Rosh distinguishes the case of heirs who say that they themselves created the improvement, where the creditor must prove otherwise because the land is already destined for his collection. The Rosh explains that the latter case concerns an apotiki, where the creditor's claim is inherently tied to the land. The Mechaber below, siman 115:5, follows the Rambam that even without a specific apotiki the heirs bear the burden regarding improvement. If so, one might reason that here too the debtor redeeming the land should be treated as the one entitled to it, leaving the creditor to prove his expense claim. That would support the Mechaber. But then in bar metzra the Mechaber should likewise place the burden on the purchaser, whereas in siman 175:7 he follows the Rosh and requires the adjoining owner to prove the price reduction. An apparent contradiction remains. The better reading is that the Rosh mentioned apotiki because that was his own legal view and therefore stated the strongest form of the case, but the conceptual distinction does not depend entirely on it. In an ordinary creditor case the creditor collects by substantive law, so the property can be regarded as standing for collection. In bar metzra, by contrast, the adjoining owner has no legal title at all without the special rabbinic enactment. Any doubt in that enactment reverts to ordinary law, leaving the purchaser in possession. This explains the Mechaber's ruling in bar metzra even while he follows the Rambam concerning heirs. The present case nevertheless seems to resemble bar metzra, which strengthens the Sema's objection: reversal of an appraisal is also only a rabbinic rule founded on upright conduct, while the creditor presently holds the land by law. The Rama creates an additional tension because below in siman 115 he follows the Rosh that without apotiki even land destined for collection remains sufficiently in the heirs' possession to place the burden on the creditor, yet here he accepts the Mechaber's statement that the creditor, who already possesses the land and can be displaced only by enactment, must prove his expense claim. The resolution is that the disputed expenses do not represent improvement embedded in the land itself. The creditor's claim is only that because he entered lawfully, the debtor who now removes him should reimburse what he spent. It is therefore an ordinary monetary claim against the debtor, not a possessory dispute over the land. The debtor can say that in a dispute among authorities the burden of proof rests on the claimant and assert kim li. The creditor's possession of the land does not allow him to hold it merely as security for this separate expense claim where the land itself contains no corresponding improvement. By contrast, when heirs say that they themselves improved the land, the very substance of the disputed value is physically in the land. Likewise in bar metzra, where the purchaser claims that the seller personally discounted the price for him, the disputed benefit concerns the value of the land itself. There the party in possession of the land has the stronger presumptive position. Here the dispute is only a separate claim for reimbursement, so the debtor as holder of the money is considered the possessor. This reconciles the rulings.

It does not return at all, etc. The Rosh writes that this applies specifically where the creditor improved the land or where land values increased. It is unreasonable that the debtor should watch throughout his life until land rises in value and then redeem the field, for that would close the door before lenders. The Shach understands the Rosh as opening with two cases and concluding with one rule: both improvement and market appreciation are treated alike, and if the debtor pays the creditor the added value the appraisal returns. He therefore disagrees with the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, which rule that where the creditor himself improved the land, the appraisal does not return at all. Maharsach had already taken the Shach's position. Yet Rabbenu Yerucham, Netiv 6, expressly states as the Shulchan Aruch does: improvement prevents reversal entirely, while ordinary market appreciation permits reversal if the debtor pays the current higher value. The Rosh's wording itself supports this distinction. If the two cases had precisely the same law, there was no need to mention improvement separately. It would follow all the more from market appreciation. Rather, improvement changes the land itself, giving it a new character, as the Sema explains. No amount of payment restores the original appraisal. With mere market appreciation the land is still the same land, and the Rosh's concern that the debtor might wait for a rise in value is fully answered by requiring him to pay the current price. The main question is the source for the Rosh's distinction. There is a proof from Bava Kamma and Bava Metzia, where the Gemara says that three categories have an improvement appraised and paid in money: a firstborn against an ordinary heir, a creditor against heirs, and a creditor against a purchaser. Rabbenu Chananel, cited by the Rashba, understands the Gemara to be exhaustive, apart from an arus whom the Rashba explains as included in the category of a wrongful possessor. If land appraised to a creditor could later be redeemed after the creditor improved it merely by paying for the improvement, there would be a fourth case: debtor against creditor in a reversed appraisal. The debtor would recover the land while the creditor receives the value of his improvement. Since the Gemara does not list such a case, the Rosh concludes that once the creditor has improved the land the appraisal does not return at all. The Rosh then adds market appreciation. segments.he: נפקד שתפס וכו' דעת הסמ"ע דנפקד יכול לתפוס משל המפקיד אפילו במקום דליכא פסידא כלל ואע"ג דלעיל אסקינן דבלי פסידא אין יכול לתפוס נפקד שאני דבלא"ה הדבר בידו וא"צ לזה דהא משתעבד מדר"ן ומותר ליתנו לב"ח שלו בדלית ליה נכסים ועיין מה שכתב' בס"ק אח"ז וא"כ פשיטא דיכול לתפוס דהא משתעבד לב"ח משא"כ בתופס בעלמא דלא משתעבד לב"ח א"כ יאמר מה לי ולך לתפוס בשביל ב"ח שלי ופסידא ליכא ופשוט. ואין להקשות קושי' מהר"ם מאיברא בהרא"ש פ"ק דגיטין דא' הולך מנה לפלוני אי הולך לאו כזכי יכול לחזור מי גרע מתופס לב"ח ותירץ מהר"ם דאיירי דליכא פסידא והרא"ש דכתב דתי' אמת וקשה הא הוי פקדון ביד השליח במסרו המשלח לידו וא"כ הא בלי פסידא יכול לתפוס ואיך יכול לחזור. דשם מיירי דב"ח אין כאן כדמשמע מלישנא דגמ' דצריך לקבל אחריות ואם המלוה כאן הוא יקבל וכשאין המלוה כאן לכ"ע א"י לתפוס בלי פסידא וא"ש:
segments.en: A bailee who seized, etc. The Sema holds that a bailee may retain the depositor's property for the depositor's creditor even where there is no anticipated loss at all. Although we concluded above that an ordinary person may not seize without anticipated loss, a bailee is different because the property is already in his hands. There is in fact an even simpler reason. The deposited property is subject to the creditor by Rabbi Natan's rule, and when the depositor has no other assets the bailee may deliver it directly to the depositor's creditor. See what I write in the following seif katan. Since the property itself is subject to that creditor, the bailee plainly may retain it for him. This differs from an ordinary outsider whose property is not itself subject to the creditor and who can therefore be told, "What connection do you have to this matter that you should seize for my creditor when no loss is anticipated?" One should not object from Maharam's answer, cited in the Rosh in the first chapter of Gittin, concerning one who says, "Take one hundred for so and so." If the expression "take" is not itself equivalent to acquisition, the sender can retract. Maharam asks why the messenger is not at least like one who seizes for a creditor, and answers that the case is one where no loss is anticipated. The Rosh accepts this answer. Yet once the sender has delivered the money to the messenger, the money is in the messenger's custody and should resemble a deposit, which according to the Sema may be retained even without anticipated loss. The answer is that the Gemara's case there concerns a situation in which the creditor is not present, as is implied by the Gemara's language requiring the messenger to assume responsibility. If the creditor were present, he himself could receive the money.

segments.he: אך ק' כי בתשובת רמב"ן סימן קי"ח פסק דאין אפטרופס יכול לעכב מעות יתומים שהגדילו בשבי' בע"ח רק יתן להם והם יפרעו ודוחק לחלק בין אפטרופס לנפקד ושם משמע דאפילו ב"ח בעיר ונראה ה"מ דיכול לתפוס כשהגיע זמן פרעון של מלוה שלו אבל כשלא הגיע זמן פרעון לכ"ע א"י לתפוס ולא נחלק הרא"ש בפ"ק דגיטין ארבינו פרץ דמחלק בין הגיע זמן פרעון ללא הגיע דדעת הרא"ש במקום פסידא אפילו לא הגיע יכול לתפוס אבל בדלית פסידא לכ"ע תוך זמן פרעון מהכ"ת יהיה יכול לתפוס וכי חנם הוקבע זמן. וראיה מהא דאמרינן סוף כתובות בזה הלוה לחמש וזה הלוהו לעשר זה גובה וזה גובה וכי יגרע תפיסתו שהמעות בידו מן תפיסת נפקד אחר. א"ו בתוך זמן לא מהני תפיסה במקום דליכא פסידא והרי זה כמו שאין המלוה בעיר דהא לא מטי זימנא לגבות וא"כ י"ל הך תשובת הרמב"ן איירי בכה"ג דלא מטי זימנא דאל"כ בלא"ה היה הבע"ח נפרע מאפטרופס:
segments.en: Where the creditor is absent, all agree that one may not retain the money for him without anticipated loss, and the case is therefore clear. However, there is a difficulty from the Ramban's responsum, siman 118, which rules that an administrator cannot retain money belonging to orphans who have reached majority in order to pay their creditor, but must give the money to the orphans and allow them to pay. It is strained to distinguish between an administrator and a bailee, and the responsum appears to involve a creditor who is present in town. It therefore seems that the right of a bailee to retain deposited property applies only after the creditor's due date has arrived. Before the due date, all agree that he may not retain it. The Rosh in the first chapter of Gittin disagrees with Rabbenu Peretz, who distinguishes between a debt that is due and one that is not due, only where anticipated loss exists. In such a case the Rosh permits seizure even before maturity. Where no loss is anticipated, however, what basis is there to seize before the agreed due date? The due date was not established without purpose. Proof may be brought from the end of Ketubot, where two people owe one another, one debt due after five years and the other after ten. The rule is that each debt is collected at its own time. The fact that one debtor already holds money ultimately owed by the other does not give him a stronger right than a bailee holding another's property. Thus, before maturity seizure is ineffective when no loss is anticipated. The Ramban's responsum can therefore be understood as involving a debt not yet due. Otherwise, if the creditor's debt were already collectible, he could in any event proceed against the administrator directly.

segments.he: אינו נעשה מטלטלין אצל בניו אין להקשות הא שילהי כתובות בשנים שלוו זה מזה וזה מזה ומת אחד והגבה ליתומים מטלטלין אמרינן דהוא אינו גובה דמטלטלין דיתמי לא משתעבדי וקשה לכאורה למה יגרע תפיסתו מאלו תפס הנפקד דאין נעשה מטלטלין אצל בניו ואם הוא בעצמו תופס המעות ונותנם ליתומים יהיו כמטלטלין דלא משתעבדי. די"ל הא אמרינן בפרק הכותב גבי עובדא דסבתא במלוגמא דשטרי דצ"ל מחיים אנו תופסים אותו ואז יוצא מכלל מטלטלין דיתמי ולכך כאן הא תפסן הנפקד מחיים של הלוה בשביל המלוה ולכך לא הוי תו מטלטלי דיתמי משא"כ שם בחיי הלוה לא אמר דתפס רק אח"כ כשמת השני ביקש לתפוס ותו לא מהני ובאמת שם אי גילה מחיים דעתו שרוצה לתפוס תו מפיק מן יתומים:
segments.en: It does not become movables in the hands of his sons. One should not object from the end of Ketubot, where two people owe one another and one dies. If the survivor then transfers movables to the deceased creditor's heirs, the Gemara says that he cannot collect his own debt back from those movables because movables of orphans are not subject to creditors. At first glance, why should his own possession be weaker than that of a bailee who seized property for the creditor, where the property does not become ordinary movables of the heirs? The answer is found in the chapter HaKotev, in the incident involving the grandmother and a bundle of documents. To prevent property from becoming ordinary movables of orphans, one must say and act during the debtor's lifetime, "I am holding this for the creditor." In our case the bailee seized during the debtor's lifetime on behalf of the creditor, so the property had already left the category of ordinary movables of the heirs. In the Ketubot case, by contrast, the surviving debtor did not declare during the other party's lifetime that he was retaining the money for his own debt. Only after the creditor died did he seek to treat the money as seized, and at that point seizure no longer helps. If, however, he had clearly manifested during the creditor's lifetime that he was retaining the money for his own claim, he would indeed be able to remove it from the heirs.

segments.he: ואם מסרו הנפקד כו' הרשב"א בב"ק על הא דאמרינן משתעבדא לך מדר"נ כתב מכאן שאם רוצה הנפקד או הלוה לשלם לב"ח של המפקיד דהרשות בידו דמשתעבד מדר"ן. וכן נראה מראב"ד עכ"ל ודייק הש"ך הואיל וסתם משמע אפילו אית ליה נכסים למלוה ומפקיד דאע"ג דל"א מדר"ן רק בדלית ליה נכסי מ"מ בזה אם רצה לפרוע לעולם הרשות בידו דשעבודא עכ"פ עליו. ובאמת המעיין ברשב"א בחדושיו יראה דקאי להדיא על מה דקאמרינן בגמ' מסרו השומר לניזק דאמר משתעבדנא לך מדר"ן מזה הוציאו דינו ושם ע"כ איירי בדלית ליה נכסי דזה הוא כל ראיה שלהם דר"ן לא שייך רק בדלית ליה נכסי הואיל ומשני תחלה בדלית לי' נכסי ואח"כ לא אמרינן אלא ע"ש הרי דמיירי הך דינא בדלית לי' נכסי וע"ז קאמר רשב"א דינו דמצי הנפקד לפרוע ש"מ דאיירי בכה"ג בדלית ליה נכסי וכך הבין הב"י דהוא הקשה על דברי רמב"ן דס"ל אם מסרם הנפקד ליד ב"ח של מפקיד דפטור והקשה הא ה"ל פורע חובו של חבירו שלא מדעתו ונתקשו בו הג"ת וכה"ג למה לא הקשה כן על דברי רשב"א הנ"ל דהעתיקו במחודש ג' ואדרבה בדברי רשב"א נאמר דמותר לכתחילה ואלו בדברי רמב"ן לא נאמר אלא דאם מסרו דאין עליו טענה ולפמ"ש לק"מ דברור דרשב"א אמרי בדלית ליה נכסי כמו שהוכיח מהך דב"ק ושם איירי בלית ליה נכסי וא"כ לק"מ מן פורע חוב דהא משתעבד מדר"ן: אבל הרמב"ן כפי הגי' שהעתיק הב"י הבעה"ת כי הגי' שלפנינו מוטעה כתב וז"ל ואי הלך הנפקד ומסרו ליד המלוה של המפקיד פטור וכו' לפי שאומר למפקיד אלו החזרתי לך היה גובה ממך ומשאר נכסייך וכי ליכא שאר נכסי נמי פטור מדר"ן כדאי' בפרק שור שנגח וכו' עכ"ל הרי דמיירי הן דאית ליה נכסי דיאמר מה נ"מ הא היה גובה מן שאר נכסים והן בדלית ליה נכסי דמשתעבד מדר"ן ובהכי ניחא מה שדייקו הג"ת וכה"ג דרשב"א מתיר לכתחילה למסור והרמב"ן לא אמרו רק אם מסר דרשב"א מיירי בדלית ליה נכסי ומשתעבד מדר"ן אף לכתחילה מותר והרמב"ן מיירי בדאית ליה למפקיד נכסי ולכך לא אמרו רק אם מסרו אבל לא לכתחילה ולכך יפה הקשה הב"י על הרמב"ן הא ה"ל פורע חובו של חבירו שלא מדעתו דהא מיירי בדאית ליה נכסי וא"ש וזה ברור ונכון.
segments.en: And if the bailee delivered it, etc. The Rashba, commenting on the statement in Bava Kamma that the property is subject to the claimant by Rabbi Natan's rule, writes that if a bailee or debtor wishes to pay the depositor's own creditor directly, he may do so because the property is subject to that creditor under Rabbi Natan's rule. The Raavad also appears to hold this way. The Shach infers from the Rashba's unqualified language that this permission applies even where the depositor himself has other assets. Although Rabbi Natan's rule is generally invoked only when the intermediate creditor has no other assets, the Shach argues that even where he does have assets the underlying lien still exists, and direct payment is therefore permitted if the bailee wishes to make it. In truth, one who studies the Rashba's novellae will see that his statement expressly comments on the Gemara's case in which the guardian delivered the property to the injured party because "it is subject to you under Rabbi Natan's rule." That Gemara necessarily concerns a debtor who has no other assets. The proof that Rabbi Natan's rule is limited to such a case comes from the Gemara itself, which initially establishes the case as one where he has no assets and afterward says, "rather," without abandoning that factual assumption. The Rashba's permission for the bailee to pay the creditor therefore refers precisely to a case in which the depositor has no other assets. The Beit Yosef understood it this way. He challenges the Ramban's ruling that if a bailee delivered the deposit to the depositor's creditor he is exempt, asking that this is merely a case of paying another person's debt without authorization. The Giddulei Terumah and Knesset HaGedolah ask why the Beit Yosef did not raise the same challenge against the Rashba, whom he cites as allowing direct payment even initially, whereas the Ramban merely says that after the bailee has paid he is not liable. According to what I have written, there is no difficulty. The Rashba speaks only where the depositor has no other assets, exactly like the Bava Kamma case from which he derives the rule. There Rabbi Natan's lien applies, so direct payment is fully authorized. The Ramban, however, according to the correct reading cited by the Beit Yosef from the Baal HaTerumot, writes: "If the bailee went and delivered it to the depositor's creditor, he is exempt, because he can say to the depositor: had I returned it to you, the creditor would have collected it from you or from your other assets; and where you have no other assets I am likewise exempt by Rabbi Natan's rule, as stated in the chapter Shor SheNagach." Thus the Ramban discusses both cases. Where the depositor has other assets, the bailee's defense is only that the creditor could have collected from those assets; where he has no other assets, Rabbi Natan's rule directly applies. This also explains why the Rashba permits payment initially while the Ramban speaks only after the bailee has already delivered the money. The Rashba's case is one of no other assets, where the bailee may pay directly from the outset. The Ramban's broader ruling includes a depositor who has other assets, and in that case he does not authorize the bailee to pay initially, but merely protects him from liability if he already did so. The Beit Yosef therefore properly challenges the Ramban from the rule of one who pays another's debt without authorization, because the Ramban includes the case where the depositor has other assets. The matter is clear and correct.

segments.he: דהא אף אם היה מחזירו כו' הקשו דלקמן בסימן קכ"ה כתבו הטור והמחבר והם מדברי בעה"ת שער נו"ן לוה ששלח מעותיו ביד השליח ליתנם למלוה שלו ועיכבן השליח כי אותו מלוה חייב לו ופסקו אע"פ שהמלוה מודה לו הרי משלח כופה לשליח ליתנם למלוה שכל זמן שלא נתנם לו לא נפטר המשלח מהחוב והוא דאית ליה נכסי אחריני דלא שייך דר"ן וזה מבואר דלא כמ"ש פה דאפילו אית ליה נכסי מצי למתפס שלו עבור מה שחייב לאחריני. ובאמת בבעה"ת הייתי אומר לחלק דבשלמא בידו פקדון של לוה הפקדון כל היכי דאיתא ברשות לוה ומפקיד קאי וא"כ שעבודא של בע"ח של המפקיד עליו כמ"ש הרשב"א דודאי שעבודא מ"מ חל אמטלטלין רק לא סמכה דעתא ולכך לא גבי מיתמי אבל מ"מ שעבודא עליה קאי ומכ"ש כשהן ביד אחרים דיותר אלים שעבודא כמ"ש התוס' בבכורות ובפרק יש נוחלין ועיין מש"ל ס"ס פ"ה. משא"כ כשהוא חייב לאחר והוא חייב לאחר והוא באופן דלא שייך ביה דר"ן א"כ ליכא לאותו ב"ח שעבודא עליו כלל דראוי לא משתעבד כלל ואין לו שום שעבוד על מה שחייב לו ועיין רשב"א סוף קידושין דזולת ר"נ אפילו כתב לו מטלטלין וקרקע דגובה מיתמי דמשתעבדי רק ל"ל קלא מן הלוה אינו גובה דלא משתעבד כלל דה"ל ראוי ע"ש ולכך אין לו יד לפרוע ולכך יכול לתובעו ממנו. אך כן י"ל בבעה"ת ובמחבר אבל בטור א"א לומר כן דהא הוא ס"ל פורע חוב של חבירו שלא מדעתו חייב הוא להחזירן לו וא"כ איך לא נפטר המשלח ממלוה שלו הא יאמר פרעתי לחוב שלך דקמודה בו וחייב אתה לשלם לי. ולכן נראה דיש לדקדק למה לא כתבו דמלוה חוזר על המשלח והמשלח על השליח אלא ברור שאם המשלח מרוצה לכך אין למלוה תביעה עליו הן מכח הנ"ל דהרי יכול לתפוס שלו בשביל ב"ח שלו כמ"ש כאן ומכ"ש לטור דפורע חובו חייב. רק מ"ש הטור דכל זמן שלא נתנם לו לא נפטר המשלח מהחוב הכוונה חובו לא פקע ואם יחזור המלוה עליו יכול לומר לו אתה חייב לי למול זה מה שפרעתי בשבילך וא"כ כל אחד יש לו חוב על חבירו וקי"ל זה גובה וזה גובה ועיין לעיל סי' פ"ה באריכות כמה נ"מ בזה וא"כ זה דנתן לשליח לפרוע למלוה שלו והשליח החזיקו לעצמו עדיין לא נתקיים צווי המשלח וכוונתו דרצונו לצאת ידי חוב נגד המלוה ולא להיות אצלו עבד לוה ועדיין הוא אצלו דקי"ל זה גובה וזה גובה וא"כ הרשות בידו לכוף לשליח להחזיר לו מעותיו דהא לא קיים עדיין רצונו וא"כ המעות עדיין בחזקתו כמקדם כי לא גמר שליחתו ויכול לחזור בו ולומר החזר לי מעותי ומה לי במה שאתה יש לך תביעה בו אני לא משעבד לך דלא שייך דר"ן והמעות עדיין שלי תן לי מעותי להחזרה וזהו שדייק הטור שכל זמן שלא נתנם לו לא נפטר כו' וא"כ עדיין לא נתקיים שליחתו דאלו נפטר הוה מקיים שליחתו וא"א לחזור משא"כ דלא נפטר א"כ יכול לחזור בו וזהו הכל ברצון המשלח וא"ש ולק"מ. וזהו באמת נראה ברור לדינא והכל נכון. והפרישה תי' דכאן אית ליה נכסים רק הם במד"ה ולכך שייך ביה מדר"ן וזהו דוחק נגד כוונת הב"י ונגד הסמ"ע גופיה דהקשה מן פורע חוב שלא מדעתו והש"ך תי' דלקמן איירי כשנתנו לשליח לא ידע דיש למלוה שלו נכסים והוא ט"ס דאדרבא פשיטא דמשתעבד ליה לכך צ"ל דכאן איירי דלא ידע ואין בזה ממש ולענ"ד נראה כמ"ש:
segments.en: For even if he had returned it, etc. The authorities ask from the ruling below in siman 125. There the Tur and the Mechaber, following the Baal HaTerumot, shaar 50, discuss a debtor who sent money through an agent to pay his creditor. The agent retained the money because that creditor himself owed money to the agent. They rule that even if the creditor admits the debt to the agent, the sender can compel the agent to deliver the money to the creditor, because until the creditor actually receives it the sender has not been discharged from his own debt. This applies where the creditor has other assets, so Rabbi Natan's rule does not operate. That ruling appears inconsistent with the present rule that even where the depositor has other assets, a bailee may retain his property on behalf of the depositor's creditor. With respect to the Baal HaTerumot and the Mechaber, one might distinguish as follows. A deposit remains the depositor's property wherever it is located. The depositor's creditor therefore has an underlying lien on it. Even with movables there is some form of lien, as the Rashba explains. The reason creditors do not collect movables from heirs is not the total absence of a lien, but that the creditor did not rely on those assets. All the more so when movables are already in another person's hands, where the lien is stronger, as Tosafot write in Bekhorot and in the chapter Yesh Nochalin. See what I wrote at the end of siman 85. By contrast, where A owes B and B owes C, but the conditions for Rabbi Natan's rule are absent, C has no lien at all on A's debt to B. A debt owed to B is merely prospective property relative to C, and prospective property is not subject to a lien. The Rashba at the end of Kiddushin writes that apart from Rabbi Natan's rule, even if the creditor's document expressly includes movables and land so that the creditor may collect movables from heirs, he still cannot collect a debt owed to the debtor by a third party, because that receivable is merely prospective property. Accordingly, in the agency case the agent has no legal hand to appropriate the money for his own claim, and the sender can demand it back. This distinction could explain the Baal HaTerumot and the Mechaber. It cannot, however, explain the Tur, because the Tur holds that one who pays another person's debt without authorization is entitled to reimbursement. If so, even if the agent's retention did not operate through Rabbi Natan's lien, why has the sender not been discharged? The agent can say, "I paid your creditor's debt on your behalf, which he admits owing me, and you are therefore obligated to reimburse me." It therefore appears necessary to read the Tur more carefully. Why do the Tur and the Mechaber not simply say that the creditor can continue to collect from the sender, leaving the sender to recover from the agent? Rather, if the sender himself is satisfied that the agent retain the money, the creditor has no claim against the sender on this basis. This follows from the present rule that a bailee may retain property for the depositor's creditor, and all the more so according to the Tur, who entitles one who paid another's debt to reimbursement. When the Tur says that "so long as the agent has not given it to the creditor, the sender is not discharged," he means that the original debt itself has not been extinguished as a matter of setoff. If the creditor sues the sender, the sender may answer, "You owe me a corresponding amount because I paid your debt," so each now has a claim against the other. We hold, however, that where two parties owe one another, each debt is independently collectible. See above in siman 85 for the many practical consequences. The sender's instruction to the agent was not merely to create a counterclaim, but to discharge him from his debt to the creditor so that he would no longer stand as a debtor to that creditor. If the agent retains the money, that purpose has not been fulfilled. The sender may therefore revoke the agency and demand return of the money. The money remains his because the agent has not completed the mission for which it was entrusted. The agent cannot answer, "I have my own claim against your creditor," because the sender never subjected these funds to the agent, Rabbi Natan's rule being inapplicable. This is why the Tur emphasizes that "so long as he has not given it to him, the sender has not been discharged." Had the sender been discharged, the agency would have been completed and he could not revoke it. Since he remains legally indebted, he can revoke the agency and recover his money. This interpretation depends on the sender's own will and resolves the apparent contradiction. It appears correct for practical halakhah. The Perishah answers that here the depositor's other assets are overseas, so Rabbi Natan's rule still applies. This is strained and contrary to the Beit Yosef's intent. The Shach answers that below the sender originally did not know that his creditor had other assets, but that is surely a scribal inversion, for if he did not know of other assets the third party lien would more readily apply. In my view the explanation above is preferable.

en_segments: A bailee who seized, etc. The Sema holds that a bailee may retain the depositor's property for the depositor's creditor even where there is no anticipated loss at all. Although we concluded above that an ordinary person may not seize without anticipated loss, a bailee is different because the property is already in his hands. There is in fact an even simpler reason. The deposited property is subject to the creditor by Rabbi Natan's rule, and when the depositor has no other assets the bailee may deliver it directly to the depositor's creditor. See what I write in the following seif katan. Since the property itself is subject to that creditor, the bailee plainly may retain it for him. This differs from an ordinary outsider whose property is not itself subject to the creditor and who can therefore be told, "What connection do you have to this matter that you should seize for my creditor when no loss is anticipated?" One should not object from Maharam's answer, cited in the Rosh in the first chapter of Gittin, concerning one who says, "Take one hundred for so and so." If the expression "take" is not itself equivalent to acquisition, the sender can retract. Maharam asks why the messenger is not at least like one who seizes for a creditor, and answers that the case is one where no loss is anticipated. The Rosh accepts this answer. Yet once the sender has delivered the money to the messenger, the money is in the messenger's custody and should resemble a deposit, which according to the Sema may be retained even without anticipated loss. The answer is that the Gemara's case there concerns a situation in which the creditor is not present, as is implied by the Gemara's language requiring the messenger to assume responsibility. If the creditor were present, he himself could receive the money.

Where the creditor is absent, all agree that one may not retain the money for him without anticipated loss, and the case is therefore clear. However, there is a difficulty from the Ramban's responsum, siman 118, which rules that an administrator cannot retain money belonging to orphans who have reached majority in order to pay their creditor, but must give the money to the orphans and allow them to pay. It is strained to distinguish between an administrator and a bailee, and the responsum appears to involve a creditor who is present in town. It therefore seems that the right of a bailee to retain deposited property applies only after the creditor's due date has arrived. Before the due date, all agree that he may not retain it. The Rosh in the first chapter of Gittin disagrees with Rabbenu Peretz, who distinguishes between a debt that is due and one that is not due, only where anticipated loss exists. In such a case the Rosh permits seizure even before maturity. Where no loss is anticipated, however, what basis is there to seize before the agreed due date? The due date was not established without purpose. Proof may be brought from the end of Ketubot, where two people owe one another, one debt due after five years and the other after ten. The rule is that each debt is collected at its own time. The fact that one debtor already holds money ultimately owed by the other does not give him a stronger right than a bailee holding another's property. Thus, before maturity seizure is ineffective when no loss is anticipated. The Ramban's responsum can therefore be understood as involving a debt not yet due. Otherwise, if the creditor's debt were already collectible, he could in any event proceed against the administrator directly.

It does not become movables in the hands of his sons. One should not object from the end of Ketubot, where two people owe one another and one dies. If the survivor then transfers movables to the deceased creditor's heirs, the Gemara says that he cannot collect his own debt back from those movables because movables of orphans are not subject to creditors. At first glance, why should his own possession be weaker than that of a bailee who seized property for the creditor, where the property does not become ordinary movables of the heirs? The answer is found in the chapter HaKotev, in the incident involving the grandmother and a bundle of documents. To prevent property from becoming ordinary movables of orphans, one must say and act during the debtor's lifetime, "I am holding this for the creditor." In our case the bailee seized during the debtor's lifetime on behalf of the creditor, so the property had already left the category of ordinary movables of the heirs. In the Ketubot case, by contrast, the surviving debtor did not declare during the other party's lifetime that he was retaining the money for his own debt. Only after the creditor died did he seek to treat the money as seized, and at that point seizure no longer helps. If, however, he had clearly manifested during the creditor's lifetime that he was retaining the money for his own claim, he would indeed be able to remove it from the heirs.

And if the bailee delivered it, etc. The Rashba, commenting on the statement in Bava Kamma that the property is subject to the claimant by Rabbi Natan's rule, writes that if a bailee or debtor wishes to pay the depositor's own creditor directly, he may do so because the property is subject to that creditor under Rabbi Natan's rule. The Raavad also appears to hold this way. The Shach infers from the Rashba's unqualified language that this permission applies even where the depositor himself has other assets. Although Rabbi Natan's rule is generally invoked only when the intermediate creditor has no other assets, the Shach argues that even where he does have assets the underlying lien still exists, and direct payment is therefore permitted if the bailee wishes to make it. In truth, one who studies the Rashba's novellae will see that his statement expressly comments on the Gemara's case in which the guardian delivered the property to the injured party because "it is subject to you under Rabbi Natan's rule." That Gemara necessarily concerns a debtor who has no other assets. The proof that Rabbi Natan's rule is limited to such a case comes from the Gemara itself, which initially establishes the case as one where he has no assets and afterward says, "rather," without abandoning that factual assumption. The Rashba's permission for the bailee to pay the creditor therefore refers precisely to a case in which the depositor has no other assets. The Beit Yosef understood it this way. He challenges the Ramban's ruling that if a bailee delivered the deposit to the depositor's creditor he is exempt, asking that this is merely a case of paying another person's debt without authorization. The Giddulei Terumah and Knesset HaGedolah ask why the Beit Yosef did not raise the same challenge against the Rashba, whom he cites as allowing direct payment even initially, whereas the Ramban merely says that after the bailee has paid he is not liable. According to what I have written, there is no difficulty. The Rashba speaks only where the depositor has no other assets, exactly like the Bava Kamma case from which he derives the rule. There Rabbi Natan's lien applies, so direct payment is fully authorized. The Ramban, however, according to the correct reading cited by the Beit Yosef from the Baal HaTerumot, writes: "If the bailee went and delivered it to the depositor's creditor, he is exempt, because he can say to the depositor: had I returned it to you, the creditor would have collected it from you or from your other assets; and where you have no other assets I am likewise exempt by Rabbi Natan's rule, as stated in the chapter Shor SheNagach." Thus the Ramban discusses both cases. Where the depositor has other assets, the bailee's defense is only that the creditor could have collected from those assets; where he has no other assets, Rabbi Natan's rule directly applies. This also explains why the Rashba permits payment initially while the Ramban speaks only after the bailee has already delivered the money. The Rashba's case is one of no other assets, where the bailee may pay directly from the outset. The Ramban's broader ruling includes a depositor who has other assets, and in that case he does not authorize the bailee to pay initially, but merely protects him from liability if he already did so. The Beit Yosef therefore properly challenges the Ramban from the rule of one who pays another's debt without authorization, because the Ramban includes the case where the depositor has other assets. The matter is clear and correct.

For even if he had returned it, etc. The authorities ask from the ruling below in siman 125. There the Tur and the Mechaber, following the Baal HaTerumot, shaar 50, discuss a debtor who sent money through an agent to pay his creditor. The agent retained the money because that creditor himself owed money to the agent. They rule that even if the creditor admits the debt to the agent, the sender can compel the agent to deliver the money to the creditor, because until the creditor actually receives it the sender has not been discharged from his own debt. This applies where the creditor has other assets, so Rabbi Natan's rule does not operate. That ruling appears inconsistent with the present rule that even where the depositor has other assets, a bailee may retain his property on behalf of the depositor's creditor. With respect to the Baal HaTerumot and the Mechaber, one might distinguish as follows. A deposit remains the depositor's property wherever it is located. The depositor's creditor therefore has an underlying lien on it. Even with movables there is some form of lien, as the Rashba explains. The reason creditors do not collect movables from heirs is not the total absence of a lien, but that the creditor did not rely on those assets. All the more so when movables are already in another person's hands, where the lien is stronger, as Tosafot write in Bekhorot and in the chapter Yesh Nochalin. See what I wrote at the end of siman 85. By contrast, where A owes B and B owes C, but the conditions for Rabbi Natan's rule are absent, C has no lien at all on A's debt to B. A debt owed to B is merely prospective property relative to C, and prospective property is not subject to a lien. The Rashba at the end of Kiddushin writes that apart from Rabbi Natan's rule, even if the creditor's document expressly includes movables and land so that the creditor may collect movables from heirs, he still cannot collect a debt owed to the debtor by a third party, because that receivable is merely prospective property. Accordingly, in the agency case the agent has no legal hand to appropriate the money for his own claim, and the sender can demand it back. This distinction could explain the Baal HaTerumot and the Mechaber. It cannot, however, explain the Tur, because the Tur holds that one who pays another person's debt without authorization is entitled to reimbursement. If so, even if the agent's retention did not operate through Rabbi Natan's lien, why has the sender not been discharged? The agent can say, "I paid your creditor's debt on your behalf, which he admits owing me, and you are therefore obligated to reimburse me." It therefore appears necessary to read the Tur more carefully. Why do the Tur and the Mechaber not simply say that the creditor can continue to collect from the sender, leaving the sender to recover from the agent? Rather, if the sender himself is satisfied that the agent retain the money, the creditor has no claim against the sender on this basis. This follows from the present rule that a bailee may retain property for the depositor's creditor, and all the more so according to the Tur, who entitles one who paid another's debt to reimbursement. When the Tur says that "so long as the agent has not given it to the creditor, the sender is not discharged," he means that the original debt itself has not been extinguished as a matter of setoff. If the creditor sues the sender, the sender may answer, "You owe me a corresponding amount because I paid your debt," so each now has a claim against the other. We hold, however, that where two parties owe one another, each debt is independently collectible. See above in siman 85 for the many practical consequences. The sender's instruction to the agent was not merely to create a counterclaim, but to discharge him from his debt to the creditor so that he would no longer stand as a debtor to that creditor. If the agent retains the money, that purpose has not been fulfilled. The sender may therefore revoke the agency and demand return of the money. The money remains his because the agent has not completed the mission for which it was entrusted. The agent cannot answer, "I have my own claim against your creditor," because the sender never subjected these funds to the agent, Rabbi Natan's rule being inapplicable. This is why the Tur emphasizes that "so long as he has not given it to him, the sender has not been discharged." Had the sender been discharged, the agency would have been completed and he could not revoke it. Since he remains legally indebted, he can revoke the agency and recover his money. This interpretation depends on the sender's own will and resolves the apparent contradiction. It appears correct for practical halakhah. The Perishah answers that here the depositor's other assets are overseas, so Rabbi Natan's rule still applies. This is strained and contrary to the Beit Yosef's intent. The Shach answers that below the sender originally did not know that his creditor had other assets, but that is surely a scribal inversion, for if he did not know of other assets the third party lien would more readily apply. In my view the explanation above is preferable.

segments.he: מצוה על היורשים לפרוע כו' וכופין אותם כו'. הטעם דהיורשים במקום אביהן קיימי וכמ"ש הטור והמחבר בסמוך מיהו ה"מ בשיעבוד קרקעות דעיקר סמיכת דעתו דמלוה עליהן ואפי' לוה ואח"כ קנה קרקע דלא סמכא דעת המלוה בשעת הלואה על קרקע זו שקנה ואם היה מכרה לאחר לא הי' המלוה טורפה מיד הלוקח כשלא כ' למלוה דאקני וכמ"ש הטור והמחבר לעיל סי' ק"ד מ"מ מהיורשים גובין אף מדין תורה מטעם שכתבתי דלא מחשבי כאחר אלא כהלוה עצמו בדבר של קיימא כגון קרקע משא"כ במטלטלים שאינו דבר של קיימא דהא יכול להבריחם ולהעלימם מעין של מלוה ומש"ה אינם משועבדים למלוה מדין תורה לכפות ליורשים שיפרעו מהם חובות אביהן אבל מ"מ משום מצות עשה דכיבוד אב יש בו שגנאי הוא לאביהם שיהא בכלל לוה רשע ולא ישלם והן ירשו את ממונו ויאכלוהו ויחדו אלא יכבדו את אביהן וישלמו חובן ממה שהניח אבל כשלא הניח אביהן כלום אין בה מצות כיבוד אב ואם שהוא דוקא בממון של אביהן ואמן וכמ"ש בי"ד סי' ר"מ ע"ש:
segments.en: Because the enactment of the later authorities does not have power to obligate orphans in such matters. The Tur likewise cites this in his name in Even HaEzer siman 100 regarding collection of a ketubah from movable property. I write this to teach that it is proper even nowadays to state such a lien explicitly in a debt instrument for this reason.

segments.he: אין כופין כו' אבל מצוה כו'. ז"ל הטור וטעמא דמצות כבוד היא מ"ע שמתן שכרה בצדה וכל מ"ע ששכרה בצדה אין ב"ד שלמטה מוזהרין עליה (?") והרמב"ן בתשובה סי' כ"ה כתב ע"ז וז"ל דמ"מ אם הב"ד רוצים לכוף הרשות בידם עכ"ל והביאו מור"ם בסי' צ"ז בסי"ו אדין מצות השבת העבוט וכאן שסתם אפשר שסמך אמ"ש לעיל בסי' צ"ז אבל קשה למה סתם בי"ד ר"ס ר"מ הדברים ולא כתב הרשות ביד ב"ד אם ירצו לכוף ואפשר שה"ט משום שהתוס' והרא"ש פליגי אהרמב"ן והביאו ראיה מגמ' דילן שמשמעותו שאין כופין כלל וזהו דלא כהירושלמי שהביא רמב"ן ראי' מיניה (אלא שהרמב"ן יש לו ישוב אמשמעות גמרא דילן וכמ"ש כל זה בדרישה ע"ש) וכיון דיש בדבר פלוגתא מש"ה בכיבוד אב ואם לא רצה מור"ם לכתוב להכריח הבן ולכפותו דהו"ל כאילו באנו להוציא מידו שיטריח נפשו במקום שיש פלוגתא בדבר משא"כ בהשבת העבוט דמשכון עומד ברשות הלוה ולא מיקרי הוצאה מידו במה שכופין אותו להשיב העבוט. ובזה מיושב נמי קצת הא דהכא דכיון דמטלטלי דיתמי מן הדין אינן משועבדין לבע"ח הרי הוא ברשות היורשים ואין כופין אותם שיוציאו וישלמו ודו"ק:
segments.en: However, according to the Tur in the name of the Rosh at the end of siman 419, regarding the rule that an injured party does not collect from the orphans' movable property under Torah law according to Rif, and according to Rabbeinu Ephraim not even by the enactment of the Geonim because that enactment was made only for lenders to avoid closing the door before borrowers, the Tur concludes that according to his father the Rosh, in these generations movable property has the status of land for every type of lien by the law of the Gemara itself, without need for the enactment of the Geonim, just as a woman's ketubah is collected from Arab camels.

segments.he: אבל הגאונים תקנו כו'. עיין בטור בסי' זה סי"ד שכתב בשם הרמב"ם ז"ל ובמערב כותבין בשט"ח שיש לו לגבות מהמטלטלים ומהמקרקעי בחייו ובמותו ונמצא גובה בשביל התנאי יותר על התקנה וסייג גדול הוא בדבר שמא לא ידע הלוה בהתקנה ונמצא גובה ממון של יתומים שלא כדין שאין כח בתקנת אחרונים לחייב בהן יתומים עכ"ל. וכ"כ הטור בשמו בא"ע סי' ק' לענין גביית כתובה מהמטלטלים ע"ש וכתבתי זה ללמד שטוב לכתוב כן בפי' בשט"ח גם בזמן הזה מה"ט מיהו לפמ"ש הטור בשם הרא"ש לקמן בס"ס תי"ט אדין דאין ניזק גובה מהמטלטלים דיתמי להרי"ף מדין תורה ולר' אפרים אפי' מתקנת גאונים דלא תיקנו הגאונים כי אם למלו' משום נעילת דלת מסיק הטור וכתב עליו ז"ל ולא"א הרא"ש ז"ל נראה דבדורות הללו מטלטלים כמקרקעי לכל מיני שעבוד מדינא דגמרא בלא תקנת הגאונים מידי דהוה אגמלא דערבא דאשה גובה כתובתה מהם עכ"ל דנראה דאליביה גם לענין גביית מלוה א"צ לכותבו בפי' ולית ביה משום חשש הרמב"ם הנ"ל:
segments.en: According to that view, even for an ordinary loan there is no need to write the lien expressly and there is no concern for Rambam's objection.

segments.he: ממלו' שהית' לאביהן ביד אחרים כו'. פירוש אע"ג דאית ביה תרתי דהן מטלטלים וגם לא הי' ביד אביהם במוחזק בשעת מותו כי אם בראוי ואין הבכור נוטל ממנו פי שנים (ע' לעיל סי' רע"ז ורע"ח) וגם יש בו חילוקים לענין גביית כתובה בא"ע סי' ק' ע"ש וגם עמ"ש לעיל ס"ס ק"ד:
segments.en: From a loan owed to their father by others, etc. Even though there are two disadvantages: it is movable property, and it was not in their father's actual possession at the time of death but merely expected to be received, so that a firstborn does not take a double portion from it. There are likewise distinctions concerning collection of a ketubah; see Even HaEzer siman 100 and what I wrote at the end of siman 104.

segments.he: בין גבו קרקע בין גבו מעות. אבל לדינא דגמ' דוקא אם גבו קרקע היו חוזרים וגובים מהם כמו שכתב הטור בסי' זה ס"ט וגם לעיל בר"ס ק"א ושם בדרישה הבאתי ל' הגמ' דאיתא שם כן ע"ש והאי גבו דמשמע דהיורשים כבר גבו ל"ד קאמר אלא אף לא גבו היורשים החוב אלא הניח שט"ח על לוין שלו הב"ח מוציא מיד היורשים השט"ח וגובה בהן דשטרות מחשבי כמטלטלים וגובה מהן וכ"כ הטור בסימן זה ובס"ס ס"ד ע"ש:
segments.en: Whether they collected land or money. Under the law of the Gemara, only if the heirs collected land could the creditor in turn collect from them. The wording "collected" is not exclusive. Even if the heirs have not yet collected the debt and their father left them promissory notes against his own borrowers, the creditor may take those notes from the heirs and collect through them, because documents are treated as movable property. The Tur states this here and at the end of siman 64.

segments.he: הדין עם היורשים הטעם כיון דמן הדין אין מטלטלים דהיורשי' משועבדי' להן כלל:
segments.en: The law is with the heirs. The reason is that under strict law the heirs' movable property is not subject to the creditors at all.

segments.he: אבל אם לא ירשו כלום כו'. אדלעיל קאי וכבר נתבאר:
segments.en: But if they inherited nothing, etc. This refers back to the preceding rule and has already been explained.
